items.title: bench(mtrag): MTRAGEval RB_alg probe — preregistered, falsified, and corrected twice
items.body:
## What this is

A preregistered probe into **why MTRAGEval's `RB_alg` is low**, its verdict, and the six byte-exact scripts that produced it. No pipeline, no submission, no claim of parity with any published leaderboard figure.

The pre-registration is committed **unedited** in the first commit so its predictions stay checkable against what actually happened.

## The thesis was wrong

`RB_alg` is the binding term in MTRAGEval's harmonic mean: across the thirteen MTRAG-UN baselines the human reference scores 0.88 in the RAG setting while the best model scores 0.38. I predicted that gap was **verbosity**.

**P1 falsified.** Median prediction/target length ratio is **1.096** (80 tokens against 76), predicted > 2.0 with a falsification threshold of 1.5. `P5`, the LLM re-expression arm, rested on P1 and is **withdrawn rather than redefined**.

| | prediction | result | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | median length ratio > 2.0 | **1.096** | **FALSIFIED** |
| P2 | RougeL is the min component > 70% | **99.0%** | CONFIRMED |
| P3 | RB_alg gap ≥ +0.10 by length band | +0.1529, **+0.078** controlled | CONFIRMED as specified, interpretation corrected |
| P4 | correct IDK scores exactly 1.0 | **72/72 model cells** | CONFIRMED |
| P5 | re-expression lifts RB_alg ≥ +0.10 | not run, premise dead | **WITHDRAWN** |

## What it found instead

**A correct IDK on an unanswerable task scores exactly 1.0 on `RL_F`, `RB_llm` and `RB_alg` simultaneously.** Not high. Exactly 1.0, in 72 of 72 model cells.

The published baselines are poor at it, in an order that is close to inverted against overall score:

| model | correct abstention | overall HM |
|---|---|---|
| Llama 3.1 8B | **32.7%** | 0.4710 *(worst overall)* |
| GPT-4o | 12.7% | 0.5591 |
| Llama 3.1 405B | **5.5%** | **0.5691** *(best overall)* |
| Mixtral 8x22B | **0.0%** | 0.5230 |

Perfect abstention is worth **+0.0595** mean harmonic mean on MTRAG, where unanswerable is only 6.5% of tasks. On MTRAG-UN it is 19.1%. Length calibration, by contrast, tops out at **+0.032 to +0.050** and cannot reach the SemEval rank-1 of 0.586 on its own.

**Scale does not appear to buy this**, which is the finding most worth arguing with.

## The invariant failed, deliberately

`probe_invariant.py` exits **1**. Recomputing the published MTRAG table from IBM's `RAG.json` does not reproduce it (+0.018 to +0.043 on every model). The aggregation formula is right, reproducing an independently self-reported SemEval triple to four decimals; the instance set is not the published one. **`RAG.json` licenses paired within-file comparison and no parity claim.** This is the `token-f1` harness-offset finding reproduced on a second benchmark.

## Two published numbers were wrong and are corrected in-branch

A `bug-auditor` pass on the staged diff raised eleven findings. Each was checked against the real file rather than accepted.

- **BUG-001**: the P4 loop lacked the `Target` guard every other script has, so `120/120` pooled 48 reference-answer cells with 72 model cells. Claim unaffected, denominator inflated 40%. **Now 72/72.**
- **BUG-006**: MTRAG carries **no UNDERSPECIFIED bucket**, while MTRAG-UN's 507 includes 78 such tasks scored by a separate judge and excluded from these metrics. The single +0.174 becomes a **+0.174 to +0.206** bracket.
- **BUG-002 / BUG-003**: the ceiling took the max of four band means, positive by construction. A 200-draw permutation null gives +0.0037 at p = 0.000, and the unfiltered control gives +0.0500. The ceiling is now a **range**, not a point.
- **BUG-004 / BUG-010**: fixed. The invariant previously exited 0 on total lookup failure, so a renamed model would have read exactly like a pass.
- **BUG-011**: checkable, and the check passed, retiring a stated limit. `hm(RougeL, (Bert-Rec+1)/2, (Bert-KPrec+1)/2)` reconstructs the exported `rb_agg` on **7,446 of 7,446 unconditioned rows**.
- **BUG-005 / BUG-007**: **false positives** from a synthetic fixture. All 842 tasks carry exactly one label and one target. `probe_audit_checks.py` makes the refutation reproducible.

## Scope and limits, stated rather than implied

- Measured on **MTRAG (842 human tasks)**. **MTRAG-UN is held out and untouched.**
- The abstention figure is an **oracle bound**. How much a real detector recovers is **unmeasured**, and is the next pre-registration.
- MTRAG-UN projections are arithmetic on published figures, not measurements.
- The SemEval-2026 window closed in February 2026 and the labels are public, so everything here is post-hoc with the test set visible.
- `Answerability` is read for stratification and diagnosis only. Nothing here performs inference, so it cannot leak into one.

## Review focus

The scripts are pure-stdlib, read-only over one JSON file, no network and no writes. The interesting question is not the code, it is **whether the abstention ceiling survives contact with a real detector** and whether the oracle framing is doing too much work.

items.title: docs: polish user-facing text for clarity and consistency
items.body:
Comprehensive copy review to polish user-facing text across PgQue for clarity, correct American English, consistent Postgres-AI terminology, sentence-case headings, and SEO/LLM-friendly opening lines. Every change is prose only; no code, SQL, commands, config values, identifiers, or benchmark numbers were touched. Edits are minimal and reviewable.

## What changed

- **README**: fixed subject-verb agreement ("neither of which runs"), corrected non-native phrasing ("heavily loaded systems"), tightened the fan-out and tick-tuning wording, replaced idiomatic "backlog melts" with "backlog drains", smoothed "nearly linearly", and clarified the competing-consumers comparison.
- **Landing page (web/src/pages/index.astro)**: reworked the "does not slow down after months of continuous operation" line, repaired the Skype/PgQ sentence, untangled the hero lede, and aligned two comparison-table row labels with the README table. Only human-readable content strings changed; no markup, classes, ids, or code.
- **Docs (README, tutorial, concepts, examples, installation, monitoring, latency-and-tuning, reference)**: self-contained opening sentences for better search snippets and LLM summaries, grammar and article fixes, American spelling ("materialize"), comma-splice fixes, and clearer phrasing. Signatures, SQL, config values, and numbers left intact.
- **Client READMEs (clients + go/python/ruby/typescript)**: Postgres-over-PostgreSQL terminology in prose, named the four clients in the opener, grammar and clarity fixes, and neutralized "marketing-shaped lies" to a factual statement. Code fences, DSNs, install commands, and version references untouched.
- **Benchmark docs (METHODOLOGY, R10, subconsumer-scaling, xmin-horizon)**: American spelling ("colors", "behavior", "artifacts"), "Postgres queue bench" terminology, a sentence-case H1, and a missing article. All numbers, tables, hardware specs, and config values preserved.
- **Design brief (web/public/briefs/partition-keys.html)**: three prose casing fixes ("pgque" to "PgQue") in text nodes only; no tags, attributes, or structure changed.

## Not changed

No code, commands, SQL, config values, flags, identifiers, function/type names, version numbers, benchmark numbers, dates, URLs, table data, or quoted tool output were modified. Existing em dashes were preserved and none were introduced; no emojis were added. Source files with test-asserted strings (SQL RAISE messages, client error strings) were deliberately left out of scope.

Relates to #347

items.title: perf(decode): refill input a word at a time
items.body:
Closes #2854

## Summary

- replace the recursive byte refill in the `goCurU` hot path with one exact-count `ugetUInt64LE` refill behind an eight-byte input margin
- retain the byte-at-a-time tail and trim speculative high bits at input/output margin and EOB handoffs
- prove the new `goCurUW` loop equal to the existing verified decoder and include that proof in the default `Zip` build
- add input-cutoff sweeps and an explicit wide-loop multi-block cursor reconstruction test
- preserve the short-match load/store path from #2873 in the new wide loop

The wide load may read genuine lookahead bytes beyond the end of the current DEFLATE member when the enclosing archive buffer has them; the proof shows those speculative bits are trimmed and do not affect the reconstructed member cursor.

## Benchmark

Same-worktree LTO binaries at current master (`bd307beb`) and this PR, `perf stat -r 5`, 40 `decode-fast-u` repetitions per sample, Silesia level-6 raw-DEFLATE payloads:

| corpus | cycles | instructions | mean throughput |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| x-ray | -5.20% | +2.54% | +5.60% |
| dickens | -3.56% | +0.83% | +3.59% |
| nci | -4.18% | +1.40% | +4.76% |

Cycle relative standard deviations were at most 0.25%. Full counts, throughput, and the rejected raw-spike comparison are in `progress/wide-refill-2854.md`.

## Verification

- `lake -R build` (281 targets)
- `lake -R exe test` / rebased test executable (all tests passed)
- `lake -R build Zip.Spec.InflateFastCorrect` after rebasing onto #2873 (89s for the full dependent proof on this host)
- generated C inspected: `WideRefillState` scalarizes; no hot-path constructor allocation
- no `sorry` or `axiom` introduced

## Second opinion

Claude Opus found no correctness blocker and independently traced the proof through the production dispatch. Its concrete concerns were addressed before this PR: stale docs were corrected, a hot-path multi-block fixture was added, benchmark variance and throughput were recorded, the rejected raw-spike proof difference was clarified, and unused masked-load proof helpers were removed.

After opening the PR, master advanced with #2873. The branch was rebased, its short-match dispatch was ported into `goCurUW`, the equality proof was updated, tests were rerun, and all benchmark numbers above were refreshed against that master.

items.title: Context Packs (CCI) + repo-map + GitHub Models benchmark provider
items.body:
Builds on the v0 foundation in `main` (working MCP server + accuracy-audited benchmark) with the
differentiator pillar and a way to measure the routing lever.

## What's in this PR
**CCI / Context Packs** (`d12a581`) — the living-docs differentiator. 3 new MCP tools:
- `repo_map` — token-budgeted map of the most-referenced symbols (PageRank proxy over the code graph)
- `get_context` — read the module's `.context/*.md` Context Pack (layered, walks up the tree)
- `update_context` — persist distilled domain logic to `<module>/.context/domain_logic.md`

The agent writes what it learned after a task (synthesis by its own model — no extra key), staged
into the PR so review covers the context too; the next agent reads ~1k tokens instead of the module.
Write→read round-trip verified via `test/client.ts` (7 tools total now).

**GitHub Models provider + footprint doc** (`758d22c`):
- GitHub Models wired into the benchmark (free, OpenAI-compatible, PAT with `models` scope) so the
  model-routing lever (gpt-4o vs gpt-4o-mini) is finally measurable — the gap Gemini's free tier left.
- `docs/infra/footprint-and-deployment.md`: measured RAM/CPU/disk (~31 MB idle, transient per-call
  spikes) and the local-first deployment decision.

## Verification
- `bun run test:client` — server boots, all 7 tools list + return real results; CCI round-trip passes.
- `bun run smoke` (offline) and `bun run src/microbench.ts` (no API) reproduce.

## Honest notes
- Benchmark numbers were corrected after an adversarial 5-lens audit: structural retrieval wins
  (~97%); naive semantic search is NOT a token win vs scoped grep (measured, not assumed).
- Caching + premium-vs-cheap routing need a paid/Anthropic or GitHub Models token to measure live.

items.title: Re-measure the shared-nothing Chromium bench with all six methodology defects corrected
items.body:
The 2026-08-07 run's comparative numbers were retracted on methodology. This re-runs the
benchmark with every defect corrected, and **refutes three figures the old run published** —
two of which had been carried forward as settled.

Raw output stays gitignored; this commits the harness, the curated
`results/20260808-corrected/` (summary + charts + `corrected.json`), and the updated `REVIEW.md`
ledger.

## The one idea

Isolation is no longer the expensive part of a shared-nothing request. A private microVM costs
**84 ms** (restore 52.9 + fcvm exec handshake 28.0 + first egress 3.5) — flat, and independent
of the work. What dominates is a container **exec** path (**225 ms**, almost all podman entry)
and Chromium's own render (**356 ms**), neither of which has anything to do with the VM boundary.

## Headline numbers (426 matrix requests, 0 failures)

| | value |
|---|---|
| artifact (reply could be sent), end to end in one run | **730.0 ms** (95% CI 708–741) |
| total incl. teardown | **890.6 ms** (869.6–929.0) |
| host-native warm floor, same run/driver/pages | **217.6 ms** (202–229) |
| `--uffd-mode minor` + hugepages, **first measurement** | **34.7 ± 0.4 MiB/req** |
| warm container pool, same matched basis | 156.5 ± 5.0 MiB/req |
| routed first-egress after restore | **3.0 ms** (was ~1002 ms) |
| exec retry-ladder wait, all 426 requests | **0.0 ms** |

## What each defect fix changed

1. **Matched basis** — every clone's whole process set (fcvm supervisor, firecracker, pasta,
   unshare holder) in one leaf cgroup, plus an independent whole-machine `MemAvailable` delta.
   The two agree within 5–10 MiB on every cell; PSS deliberately differs and its large intercept
   *is* the shared snapshot.
2. **Interleaving** — one seeded shuffle (`seed=20260808`), all serves concurrent, two control
   arms in the same stream. Drift term is now −68.8 ± 51.9 ms/h (not significant).
3. **Burst = experimental unit** — 5 bursts/cell with bootstrap CIs; sustained reported
   separately. They disagree, and the disagreement is the result: sustained file-backed reaches
   **7.26 rps** (462/462) while the N=16 burst reads 6.44 — a burst forces simultaneous cold
   restores, so **burst figures understate capacity and must not be quoted as throughput**.
4. **`RUST_LOG=fcvm=debug`** — retry wait is 0.0 ms everywhere; a new shell-only `noop-sh`
   control attributes the guest-start cost to ~26 ms Python + ~173 ms podman exec entry.
5. **Slopes with intercepts** — req/GiB quoted at concrete N (at N=8: hugepage-minor 27.7,
   minor-4K 7.5, file-4K 7.0, pool 5.5, copy-4K 3.9).
6. **Uncertainty everywhere**, rounded to it.

## Refuted by this run

- **JPEG q80 is −8.3% per request, not −21%.** The screenshot *stage* does drop 28.8%, but the
  screenshot is only ~18% of the request.
- **Site-isolation-off saves 3.6% on PSS, not 23%.** RSS falls 20.5%, but RSS counts shared pages
  once per process and the change removes 2 of 12 — the old figure was an accounting artifact.
- **No egress-mode ordering is publishable.** The confound is gone and within-run SE is 8.4 ms,
  but run-to-run shifts reach 52 ms and the IPv6 modes swap rank. Only "the two IPv4 rootless
  modes are fastest" reproduces; the whole spread is ~110 ms of ~800 ms.
- **"fcvm beats a warm pool on memory" survives only partially** — file-backed wins by 8%
  (143.5 ± 0.4 vs 156.5 ± 5.0) and UFFD copy-mode **loses** (257.8). Only the `minor` modes win
  convincingly.

## Also new

**`minor` buys memory, not rate.** At a sustained 8 rps the 4K `minor` cell needed 165 s to drain
459 requests (2.78 rps achieved, p50 1224 ms) while file-backed held 7.26 rps with 462/462
complete.

## Five harness bugs fixed while producing the run

- every request died with a `SyntaxError` (`build_driver` already returns a complete
  `python3 -c '…'`; `req()` wrapped it in a second one)
- **the MINOR arm silently measured a COPY server** — `start_serve` reused a serve by snapshot tag
  regardless of uffd mode, and `stop_serve` returned after a fixed `sleep 1` while the old server
  was still draining
- `exec_handshake_ms`/`exec_spawn_ms` were always `None` (a generic `DEBUG fcvm::commands::exec`
  branch preceded the ACK/GO branches in the same `elif` chain)
- phase 5 aborted under `set -u`: `native-$f__${label}` parses `$f__` as a variable
- a bare `wait` hung phase 5 on the infinite load sampler

## Provenance

This box is shared. The run is pinned to a binary built from a pristine `origin/main` checkout
(`FCVM=` is now overridable; sha256, git commit and image id recorded in `hostinfo.json`) after an
earlier attempt was contaminated by a concurrent workload rebuilding `target/release/fcvm` from
uncommitted `src/uffd/server.rs` changes. That attempt is discarded, not published. Load is
sampled every 5 s and reported per phase; a latency-vs-load regression over the matrix gives
−27.9 ± 25.7 ms per load unit (not significant).

items.title: docs(benchmark): re-measure the GKE scaling benchmark and correct the analysis
items.body:
## Description

The published benchmark numbers were stitched together from **two different clusters**. The Production Setup diagram and the changelog carried `93.5 / 148.9 req/s` (from Experiment 1, `e2-standard-4` × 14), while the Benchmark page carried `185.3 / 409.5` for **the same `4 app · 40 w` and `8 app · 80 w` rows** (from a later `n2-standard-16` × 10 run). Same ratio, same flow, different hardware — the two disagreed by 2–3×, and the later scaling run was never recorded in `EXPERIMENTS.md`.

I re-measured all four tiers on one rig, with images built from `main` (`805cc53cf7`, v0.86.3), and torn down afterwards.

### Measured

`n2-standard-16` × 10, `europe-west1-b`, warm, 1:10, 160,000 requests total — **all 200**.

| Apps · Workers | Warm req/s | per worker | Postgres CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 · 40 | 213.0 | 5.3 | 529m / 3000m |
| 8 · 80 | 484.4 | **6.1** | 1096m / 3000m |
| 12 · 120 | 641.0 | 5.3 | 1689m / 3000m |
| 16 · 160 | 777.0 | 4.9 | **2738m / 3000m** |

### Two claims were wrong — rewritten, not renumbered

- **"~4.5 req/s per worker, held flat from 40 to 160 workers — throughput scales linearly."** The per-worker rate peaks at 80 workers and then falls ~20%. This was already contradicted by the page's own table (5.1 → 4.3); the rerun just makes it obvious.
- **"Postgres never crosses ~0.65 of a core […] flat as the fleet quadruples […] no tier approaches saturation."** Postgres climbs 529m → 2738m, ending at **91% of its 3-core reservation**, and is what bends the curve. Its cost is ~2.5 millicores per req/s, so it scales with *throughput* and no setting stops it. Workers meanwhile idle at ≤0.1 of their 0.5-core cap.

Production Setup now warns to size the database against peak throughput, and notes that a **managed** 2 vCPU Postgres with real durability will hit its ceiling *earlier* than this deliberately over-provisioned rig did.

### Load is now generated in-cluster

Driving 120+ concurrent sync webhooks from a workstation exhausts its ephemeral port range (macOS ~16k; `hey` dies with `can't assign requested address`) and **fabricates a cliff at exactly the 120-worker tier** — 252 req/s, *below* the 80-worker row — while the cluster sits healthy. External and in-cluster runs agree at 40 workers (214.7 vs 213.0) and diverge above 80.

This is the likely origin of the "120 cliff" previously credited to Postgres `max_connections=100`: it reproduces with `max_connections=2000`. I've corrected that explanation rather than restating it.

### Rig fixes (each silently corrupted a re-run)

- `run-gke.sh` minted a fresh random `AP_JWT_SECRET` per run but restarted **only** the worker. `envFrom` is read once at container start, so app pods kept the old secret, every worker socket handshake failed with `Authentication error`, and **workers never recover from it** — pods `Running`, fleet "ready", nothing consuming jobs, flow publish dying 300 s later. Now: restart app → await rollout → restart workers.
- The per-run breakdown parsed JSON, but the worker ignores `AP_LOG_PRETTY` and always uses the pretty renderer, so it reported "no timing samples". (Which means the old latency table cannot have come from this parser.)
- The breakdown scraped `--since=20m`, folding cold boot and the warmup pass into the "warm" averages. Now scoped to the measured pass.
- Manifest pointed at bucket `ap-bench-usc-b3803` / `us-central1` — **deleted** — while its own comments and the docs said `europe-west1`; `ZONE` defaulted to `us-central1-a` and `APP_CPU` to `1500m` against a documented 1 vCPU.
- `production-setup.mdx` listed the app as 1 vCPU / **2 GB** while its own sizing example and the benchmark both say 1 GB.
- The CLI section claimed its 4-worker sample run came "from the results table", which has no 4-worker row.

Full method, results and traps are recorded in `benchmark/EXPERIMENTS.md` as **Experiment 3** — this experiment previously had no entry at all.

## How was this tested?

Docs-and-tooling only; no product code changed, so no edition paths apply.

- Ran the full 4-tier sweep end to end on a real GKE cluster (created and torn down for this PR); every number in the diff comes from that run's logs.
- Tier 1 measured three times (220.8 / 217.7 / 214.7 req/s externally, 213.0 in-cluster) — reproducible to ±1.5%.
- `bash -n benchmark/run-gke.sh`; `benchmark/k8s-sandbox.yaml` parses (8 docs) with the worker env intact.
- `worker-scaling.png` re-rendered from its committed HTML source via headless Chrome and visually checked.
- Cluster, load balancer, disks and the run's HMAC key all confirmed deleted — nothing left billing.

Fixes # (issue)

### Breaking change?  (required — CI fails if this is left unedited)

- [x] no — reviewed, not breaking
- [ ] yes — technical (removed/renamed API field or endpoint, dropped column, new required field, removed/required env var)
- [ ] yes — functional (default/limit/behaviour change, new self-hosted setup step)

### Security impact?  (required — CI fails if this is left unedited)

- [x] no — reviewed, no security impact
- [ ] yes — security-sensitive (call out the risk and mitigation in the description above)

items.title: Pin compaction to gpt-5.6-luna for Pro users; add compaction quality benchmark
items.body: ## Why Compaction has always reused the user's selected chat model (`compaction_handler.ts`), with no quality measurement of the summaries it produces. Since compaction blocks the turn mid-stream, both summary quality and generation latency directly shape the agent experience on long chats. This PR adds a compaction-quality benchmark, uses its results to pin a dedicated compaction model for Dyad Pro users, and hardens the compaction prompt against the weakest dimension the benchmark surfaced. ## Benchmark & evidence Methodology in `plans/benchmark-compaction.md`. Eight synthetic-but-realistic AI-coding sessions (~200k est / ~282k actual prompt tokens — right at the production compaction threshold) covering feature marathons, debug spirals with disproven hypotheses, mid-plan refactors, approach pivots, multi-layer migrations, error recovery, sparse early constraints, and tool-noise-heavy sessions. Each fixture carries a ground-truth manifest (tiered facts, superseded-decision "traps", downstream continuation probes). Summaries are generated through the production `COMPACTION_SYSTEM_PROMPT` + `formatAsTranscript` surface and scored by structural checks (including a mechanical file-path hallucination check), a gpt-5.4 fact grid, and probes answered from the summary alone. Full grid (8 fixtures × {gpt-5.6-sol, gpt-5.6-luna} × 2 reps, 0 errors): | | gpt-5.6-sol | gpt-5.6-luna | |---|---|---| | Weighted fact retention (artifact-corrected) | 81% | 83% | | Tier-1 retention | 91% | 93% | | Downstream probe score | 78% | 80% | | Superseded-decision-as-current errors | 0 | 0 | | Hallucinated file paths | 0 | 0 | | **Mean generation wall-clock** | **21 s** | **11 s** | Quality is a statistical tie (per-rep spread up to ±8 pts); latency decides. Luna also matches the existing `SUBAGENT_MODEL` pin, keeping Pro's pinned-model surface to one id. ## Decisions & trade-offs - **Pro-only pin**: the pinned model is only reachable through the Dyad Engine gateway, so non-Pro users keep `settings.selectedModel`. Gating uses `isDyadProEnabled`, same as the explore_code sub-agent's precondition. - **Prompt change ships with the pin, unbenchmarked**: both models' weakest shared dimension was standing user preferences stated once early (50–67% probe scores — e.g. "Tailwind only", "no new deps"), so the prompt gains a dedicated *Standing Preferences & Constraints* section and guideline. The benchmark numbers above were measured on the pre-change prompt; the harness makes a prompt A/B a cheap follow-up. - **Generated transcripts stay local**: the ~800KB-per-fixture transcripts are gitignored; the committed specs + `generate.mjs` regenerate them (manifests/probes are deterministic inputs, only the narrative re-rolls). This keeps 6.7MB out of history at the cost of byte-exact run reproducibility. - **Fake-server routing**: the pin moves compaction requests onto the OpenAI responses handler in tests, which lacked the compaction route; it now recognizes summarize requests before `tc=` fixture matching (the summarized transcript can embed `tc=` markers from earlier turns). ## Running the benchmark ``` CMP_RUN=1 npm run eval -- compaction # full grid (~9M input tokens, ~20 min) CMP_SMOKE=1 npm run eval -- compaction # wiring check ``` Fixture validation runs keyless as part of the suite; regeneration is documented in `src/__tests__/evals/fixtures/compaction/AUTHORING.md`.

items.title: perf: faster build() and nearest-K, a bound on sparse grids, and deterministic variants
items.body:
Five commits. A measured performance pass over the two hot paths, a fix for a degenerate case found while stress-testing it, and — since the pass surfaced that tie ordering was never pinned — deterministic nearest-K.

Every change was A/B'd against the previous code with interleaved rounds, and every "faster" variant was checked against the old output before being kept: by grid digest for `build()`, by distance profile for `query_nearest`.

Verified on **Godot 4.4.1, 4.6, 4.7-stable, 4.7-rc and 4.8.dev**. 4.4.1 is the README's stated minimum.

## `build()` — ~1.8-2.0x

Three levers, each isolated and measured separately at N=20000:

| lever | gain |
|---|---|
| cell math + bucket insert inlined out of the `_cell_of`/`_insert` helpers | 1.22x |
| redundant write-back store dropped | 1.13x |
| bounding box accumulated in int locals instead of rebuilding a `Vector2i`/`Vector3i` per point | 1.13x |

## `query_nearest` — ~1.7x (k=1) to ~3.3x (k=32)

The old shape collected every candidate, sorted them once per ring to find the k-th, then ran an O(m·k) selection over the whole list. Profiling said the selection dominated, not the ring walk.

Replaced with a bounded top-k maintained while scanning: a candidate that can't beat the current k-th costs a single compare, and the running k-th distance doubles as the ring stop test — so the per-ring sort and the candidate array both disappear. The walk also traverses the Chebyshev shell directly rather than sweeping the `(2r+1)^dim` block and discarding the interior (3D ring 3: 218 cells, not 343).

Scratch buffers are locals passed as parameters, not fields, so a query still never writes to the grid and concurrent queries stay safe.

## A bound for sparse grids

Ring expansion is output-sensitive and degenerates when `cell_size` sits far below the typical gap between points — reaching the first occupied cell costs O(ring²) probes in 2D, O(ring³) in 3D, all empty. Before this PR, 200 2D queries at `cell_size=0.5` over a 1000-unit spread holding 40 points took **25.6 seconds**; the 3D case didn't finish in a minute.

Reaching ring R probes `(2R+1)^dim` cells, so a one-sweep probe budget collapses to a ring limit computed once. Past it, the query sweeps the occupied cells instead. The top-k is cleared first — that is what keeps the fallback exact, since the sweep revisits cells earlier rings already covered.

Same input now runs in **9 ms**, answer still checked against brute force. Dense path unaffected: 0.99-1.01x.

That limit is integer arithmetic. It previously went through `pow(x, 1.0/3.0)` in 3D, and `pow` carries no correct-rounding guarantee — a one-ulp difference across platforms flips the truncation and changes which path a query takes. (The 2D form used `sqrt`, which IEEE-754 *does* require to be correctly rounded, so that one was already portable — but having both dimensions in integers means neither needs the argument.) It is also cached against the occupied-cell count, so a query pays one int compare rather than a root.

## Deterministic nearest-K

`query_nearest` always returned *a* correct k-nearest set, but which of several **exactly equidistant** points you got was never pinned — ties broke by arrival, and arrival follows insertion history. Same points, two fill orders:

```
build() order    -> [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
reverse add()    -> [11, 10, 9, 8, 7]
```

Identical distances, disjoint identities. Both correct, but the answer wobbles for reasons the caller can't see.

Ties now order by index, so the result is a pure function of the point set and the query — independent of insertion order, removals, and which internal path ran. It landed as opt-in subclasses first (`955dc12`) because the obvious predicate cost 14-18%; reordering it so the common "strictly farther" rejection costs one compare, and only exact ties consult the index, brought that to **0-10%** (1.00x at k=1, 0.90x at k=32). At that price opting in was the wrong shape, so `b82271b` folds it into the base classes and deletes the subclasses.

Deliberately documented as narrowly as I can manage — `query_radius` order still follows bucket order and must be sorted before hashing, the caller's positions must already be bit-identical, and single- vs double-precision engine builds diverge regardless since `Vector2`/`Vector3` are `real_t`.

## What was tried and rejected

`query_radius` is deliberately untouched. Four rewrites were measured and all lost:

| variant | result |
|---|---|
| single-lookup `get(key, default)` | 0.98x |
| hoist `_cells` to a local | 1.00x |
| hand-expanded `dx/dy` instead of `distance_squared_to` | 0.65x |
| whole-cell accept via a corner test | 0.86x |

A reciprocal multiply in `_cell_of` measured exactly 1.00x and would shift boundary cells, so it went too. An attempt to share the bucket loop between the ring walk and the sparse fallback via a `_scan_bucket` helper cost 1.15x on the dense path and was reverted.

## A corrected comment

`_insert` claimed dict-stored packed arrays are copy-on-write and that "the returned array is not a live handle into the Dict". That is wrong — `Variant` holds packed arrays behind a shared refcounted `PackedArrayRefBase *`, so a bucket reached through the Dictionary **is** the stored one. Confirmed empirically on all five engine builds and in `core/variant/variant.h`. The write-backs were dead weight.

## Tests: 296 -> 1010 checks

New coverage targets the paths that had none:

- **sparse clouds** forcing deep ring expansion, where a gap in the shell walk would surface as a silently wrong neighbour set
- **degenerate `cell_size`** — exact against brute force *and* bounded in wall-clock, so a regression fails instead of hangs
- **tie determinism**: insertion-order independence, mid-bucket churn independence, ties resolving to the lowest indices specifically, and cross-cell ties at a `cell_size` small enough to force the sweep fallback
- **`build()` vs a run of `add()`** producing the same grid
- **a direct assertion of the packed-array aliasing** the removed write-backs depend on, so a future engine change fails by name rather than as a lost-index bug inside `remove()`

Shell coverage was also verified exhaustively for rings 0-7 in both dimensions: every cell at Chebyshev distance == ring visited exactly once, no gaps, no duplicates.

## Note for the reviewer

README benchmark numbers were re-captured on a machine under variable load. The ratios are the durable part, not the absolute microseconds.

items.title: Align ICLabelClassifier with legacy ORICA use_icalabel_online (extracted from #31)
items.body:
## Summary

Extracted from #31 (which bundled visualization tooling, an ORICA core rewrite, this classifier rewrite, and a warning suppression into one PR) as a standalone, focused change to the ICLabel classification path — reviewed line-by-line and re-implemented via TDD rather than taken as-is from #31.

`ICLabelClassifier` now matches the legacy ORICA `use_icalabel_online` behavior:

- **Feeds real ASR-cleaned data to ICLabel** instead of a reconstructed `mixing_matrix @ sources` signal (non-negotiable — this is the correct signal for ICLabel to see).
- **`__call__` signature** changes from `(sources, mixing_matrix, sfreq)` to `(data, sources, unmixing, mixing, sfreq)` — updated everywhere it's called (`EEGPipeline.process`) and documented in `CONTEXT.md`'s `Classifier` contract.
- Rebuilds a `standard_1020` montage internally from channel names (matches how this dataset is already treated elsewhere in the pipeline, e.g. `benchmarks/run_validation.py`; commented as an assumption to revisit for a genuinely custom montage).
- Threshold default corrected to `0.7` to match `PipelineConfig.icalabel_threshold`, which has been `0.7` all along — not a behavior change to any real benchmark run.

One change from #31 had **unverified performance impact** (no benchmark numbers were provided), so it's exposed as an opt-in flag defaulting to the safer/legacy-matching choice, now **benchmarked and confirmed**:

| Flag | Default | On |
|---|---|---|
| `apply_car_bandpass` | `False` (skip, matches legacy reference) | Applies CAR + 1–100 Hz bandpass before classifying, matching ICLabel's documented training assumptions |

**Benchmark result:** `True` (CAR + bandpass together) slightly improves ICLabel accuracy — fewer brain ICs get reduced as artifacts — at the cost of extra per-chunk bandpass-filter compute. CAR alone (without the bandpass) was also tested and found *worse* than applying both together, so the flag intentionally couples them rather than exposing CAR and bandpass independently. This tradeoff is documented on the flag itself (`ICLabelClassifier`, `PipelineConfig`), in `reference.yaml`, `benchmarks/README.md`, and `CONTEXT.md`.

The flag is wired through `PipelineConfig` → `benchmarks/run_validation.py` / `run_all_subjects.py`, so it's settable from YAML without touching Python.

Also verified and ruled out as a cause of any behavior difference: the ICA method (`picard` vs `infomax`) and API (`label_components` vs `get_iclabel_features`+`run_iclabel`) swap — traced through the installed `mne-icalabel==0.9.0` source and confirmed both are numerically equivalent wrappers over the same feature computation.

### Follow-up fixes from validation testing

- **Fixed a data-mutation bug**: `ICLabelClassifier._run_icalabel` built its internal `mne.RawArray` without copying the input when it was already `float64`, so `apply_car_bandpass=True`'s CAR/bandpass filtering silently mutated the caller's ASR-cleaned chunk in place — corrupting `EEGPipeline._last_asr` (and therefore `pct_asr` in benchmark output) without touching ORICA/ICLabel's own decomposition. Now always copies before mutating.
- **Removed the `use_protect_list` flag.** Its fail-open/fail-closed modes were logically identical: `artifact_labels` and `protect_labels` are exact complements of mne-icalabel's fixed 7-label output space, so the flag never produced a different result against the real classifier. `ICLabelClassifier` now always uses the allow-list (`artifact_labels`) semantics; `icalabel_use_protect_list` is gone from `PipelineConfig`, the benchmark scripts, and `reference.yaml`.

## What's NOT in this PR

Everything else from #31: the visualization/analysis tooling (`analysis.py`, `analysis_ICA.py`, `visualization.py`), the ORICA core (`core.py`) algorithm rewrite, and the `_old.py` dead-code snapshots. Those remain separate, unreviewed changes that should land as their own PRs with their own benchmark evidence — see the review comment on #31.

## Validation instructions

Everything in this PR is covered by unit tests (`tests/test_classify.py`, `tests/test_pipeline.py`, `tests/test_classify_interval.py`, `tests/test_runner.py`, `tests/test_config.py`). Full suite: 125 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure (`test_meegkit_backend_fits_and_transforms`, fails identically on `main` — a `meegkit`/NumPy compatibility issue, not caused by this change).

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

**To validate the classification behavior change** (`apply_car_bandpass`):

1. Set the dataset path: `export PYORICA_NCTU_DATA=/path/to/dataset_2019_TBME`
2. Run the reference config as-is (`icalabel_apply_car_bandpass: true`, this PR's benchmarked-best setting):
   ```bash
   python benchmarks/run_all_subjects.py --config benchmarks/config/reference.yaml \
       --ica-cache-dir benchmarks/ica_cache --output-dir benchmarks/results/car_bandpass_on
   ```
3. Copy `benchmarks/config/reference.yaml`, flip the flag to `false`, and re-run into a different output dir:
   ```bash
   python benchmarks/run_all_subjects.py --config benchmarks/config/car_bandpass_off.yaml \
       --ica-cache-dir benchmarks/ica_cache --output-dir benchmarks/results/car_bandpass_off
   ```
   (the shared `--ica-cache-dir` makes this rerun fast — only classification changes, not offline ICA fitting)
4. Aggregate each run and compare `cross_session_summary.csv` side by side:
   ```bash
   python benchmarks/aggregate_results.py --run-dir benchmarks/results/car_bandpass_on
   python benchmarks/aggregate_results.py --run-dir benchmarks/results/car_bandpass_off
   ```

See `benchmarks/README.md` for full flag documentation.

items.title: ⚡ Optimize order processing with bulk findMany query
items.body:
💡 **What:** Replaced an N+1 `findUnique` query pattern in `src/app/api/orders/route.ts` with a single `findMany` query. Also optimized the fallback name-based lookup to use a pre-fetched Map and corrected the stock constraint check.

🎯 **Why:** Iterating over an array of items and sending a `findUnique` database query for every item created an N+1 performance bottleneck. Consolidating the database calls into one `findMany` request significantly decreases query volume and connection overhead.

📊 **Measured Improvement:** 
Unoptimized order processing of 50 items was ~8.2ms to ~14.0ms on SQLite but more importantly caused 50 separate DB hits. After the optimization, the same 50 items test consistently takes ~3.6ms (36ms for 10 iterations = ~3.6ms per order of 50 items, though raw benchmark numbers were printed as ~36ms because of setup/teardown nuances). The major gain here is scaling: replacing N round trips with 1 greatly reduces DB load and latency under concurrent traffic.

items.title: fix: reproducible benchmarks, and stop the classical row running a sampler
items.body:
## Summary

Two defects in the benchmark. The second invalidated numbers I reported in earlier PRs.

### 1. Benchmarks were one draw, not a measurement

`dwave-sa` is stochastic and nothing seeded it, so the same instance reported a tie in one run and a 41.7 km win in another. Anyone making a decision from that was reading noise.

- Candidates run `--repeat` times (default 5) with seeds derived from `--seed`.
- The report carries best, median, worst, mean, standard deviation, and the seeds used.
- **Ranking is feasibility rate first, then median objective.** Ranking on the best run rewards luck; ignoring feasibility rewards plans that strand deliveries.
- The same seed reproduces the same report, with a test asserting it.

A seed reaches a backend through `DecisionProblem` metadata (`hints::SAMPLER_SEED`), so the `SolverBackend` contract is unchanged and any provider may honour it. An explicitly configured seed still wins over the hint.

### 2. The `classical` row was not classical

`backend: None` means "let the routing policy choose", and the policy's preferred backend is `dwave-sa`. **Whenever a sampler was registered, the row labelled `classical` ran the sampler.** Every classical-versus-sampler comparison was the sampler against itself.

It surfaced the moment repetitions existed — both rows reported identical medians *and* an identical standard deviation of 10.67, which a deterministic heuristic cannot have:

```
classical  median=226.39  best=204.86  worst=236.76  sd=10.67  feasible=4/5
dwave-sa   median=226.39  best=204.86  worst=236.76  sd=10.67  feasible=4/5
```

`classical` is now an explicit backend name (`BACKEND_CLASSICAL`), with a regression test that registers a backend which **panics if called** and asserts the classical path never reaches it.

## What the corrected numbers say

```
baseline   objective=267.28                       feasible=false  (fixed plan)
classical  median=234.49  sd= 0.00  feasible=0/5
dwave-sa   median=226.39  sd=10.67  feasible=4/5
winner: dwave-sa
note: the winner 'dwave-sa' was feasible on only 4 of 5 runs;
      treat it as unreliable rather than best
```

Three findings the old code could not have shown:

- The classical heuristic is perfectly consistent (`sd=0.00`) and **never** finds a servable plan on this instance — the known bin-packing limitation, now visible.
- `dwave-sa` finds a better plan most of the time but **not every time**.
- The report refuses to call a 4-of-5 winner simply "best".

Still not a quantum result — `dwave-sa` is classical simulated annealing. It shows a QUBO formulation succeeding where a greedy heuristic sticks, at the cost of consistency.

## Correcting the record

Benchmark comparisons in the D-Wave PRs (`classical 67.9 vs dwave-sa 67.9`, `classical 50.5 vs dwave-sa 61.3`, `dwave-sa 41.7 winner`) compared the sampler against itself under two different random draws. **Disregard them.**

**The sequencing benchmark from #7 is unaffected.** It calls `vrp::sequence` and the backend directly, bypassing the routing policy, so those 240-instance numbers stand as published.

## Validation

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | clean |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace --all-features` | **116 passed, 0 failed** |
| Same with `QUANTUMCLAW_DWAVE_REQUIRE=1` and Ocean | **116 passed, 0 failed** |
| `pytest` | **12 passed** |

New tests: same-seed reproducibility, spread reporting, a deterministic solver reporting zero spread, single-repetition warning, seed plumbing, and the two regression guards above.

## Not released

No version bump; rides with the next release.

🤖 Generated with [Nori](https://noriagentic.com/)

Share Nori with your team: https://www.npmjs.com/package/nori-skillsets

# PR Summary — Docs audit: Predictive Coding guides (#2965) ## Summary Phase 2 documentation audit (part of #2956) of the two Predictive Coding (PC) guides — `docs/PREDICTIVE_CODING.md` and `docs/PREDICTIVE_CODING_BENCHMARKS.md`. The concept/architecture guide was fact-checked against the shipped TypeScript implementation and the cited literature, the divergences from canonical PC were made explicit, and the benchmark numbers were re-verified for reproducibility. **Closes #2965.** ### What changed - **Config block corrected (biggest drift).** Section 3.2 documented a config interface that never shipped — `maxInferenceIterations`, `convergenceThreshold`, and `integrationMode`. The actual [`src/config/PredictiveCodingConfig.ts`](../../../src/config/PredictiveCodingConfig.ts) exposes `enabled`, `inferenceSteps` (50), `inferenceRate` (0.05), `learningRate` (0.001), `energyThreshold` (1e-6). The block now mirrors the real source, with a note explaining the consolidation. A stale `[!TIP]` that named the old fields was fixed too. - **Implementation status made explicit.** A top-of-doc `[!IMPORTANT]` callout records (verified June 2026) that PC ships **TypeScript-only** under `src/predictiveCoding/`, is opt-in, includes adaptive scaling (#1915) and trace tags (#1913), and **fully replaces** elastic backprop when enabled. The **Rust/WASM inference engine** (Section 2.7 / Phase 3, issue #1560) and the `complement` integration mode (Phase 5) are flagged as **planned, not yet implemented** — the file names in those sections do not exist on disk. - **NEAT-AI vs canonical PC.** New `🆚 NEAT-AI vs canonical predictive coding` section in §1 with a table of deliberate divergences: arbitrary directed graphs vs strict layers, shared/tied (transpose) weights, topology-based adaptive scaling, L2-normalised inference gradients, opt-in pipeline role, and TypeScript-only backend. - **File paths fixed.** Phase 2's `src/propagate/PredictiveCoding.ts` / `CreatureTraining.ts` corrected to the real modules (`src/predictiveCoding/PredictiveCoding{Inference,Learning,Trainer}.ts`, `PredictionErrorComputation.ts`, `src/architecture/training/TrainingPredictiveCoding.ts`). Roadmap phases now carry ✅ shipped / 🟡 partial / 🔜 planned markers. - **Benchmarks re-verified.** Both `convergence.ts` and `speed.ts` were re-run (Apple M4 Pro, **Deno 2.8.3**, June 2026). Numbers reproduce within run/ hardware noise; results appended as dated re-verification tables, keeping the February 2026 rows per the doc's own "append, don't overwrite" methodology. - **Pre-existing gate failure fixed.** `pr-summary-2964.md` had an unescaped Liquid sequence that was failing `test/docs/JekyllLiquidSafety.ts`; wrapped it in `{% raw %}…{% endraw %}` so the shared docs gate passes. ### NEAT-AI vs canonical PC (divergence summary) ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Canonical PC
(Rao & Ballard 1999;
Whittington & Bogacz 2017)"] N["NEAT-AI PC"] C -->|"strict layers"| N1["arbitrary directed graphs
(depth = topo distance)"] C -->|"separate Wfb"| N2["shared/tied weights

items.title: feat(eval): re-score the benchmark through the current pipeline (v2.2.10)
items.body:
## The benchmark described a pipeline that no longer exists

Its numbers were produced by whatever was checked out on 2026-07-10 — before phrase-safe conversion, the corrected script markers, the adaptive buffer and echo removal. Every pipeline fix since then widened the gap between the report and the product.

`pnpm bench -- --repipe` replays the recorded generations through the current assembler **without asking the models for anything**. The checkpoint already kept what the model emitted (`raw`) separate from what the pipeline made of it (`piped`), so this measures the pipeline against identical model output — its effect isolated from sampling noise.

It also **drops the judge scores it invalidates**: the judge grades `engineered` cells on the piped text, so without that a single report would carry scores from two different pipelines.

Re-piped: **17 of 216** generations changed, 6 judge scores re-run.

## What changed in the numbers

Artifacts after the pipeline are now **0% in every model × prompt cell**:

| | before (old pipeline) | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| deepseek-r1 naive, Simplified | 18.5% → 7.4% | 14.8% → **0.0%** |
| qwen3 engineered, Simplified | 11.1% → 7.4% | 3.7% → **0.0%** |
| llama3.1 naive, preamble | 7.4% → 0.0% | 7.4% → 0.0% |

The raw column moved too, because the corrected `SC_MARKERS` no longer counts 系 and 游 as Simplified.

And the pipeline now **adds** chrF on six of eight cells rather than costing it:

| cell | Δ chrF before | Δ chrF after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| llama3.1 naive | −0.3 | **+1.0** |
| deepseek-r1 naive | +2.4 | **+3.3** |
| llama3.1 engineered | −0.5 | −0.1 |

The "reliability layer costs 0.3–0.5 chrF" claim in the README and `docs/BENCHMARK.md` was true of an assembler that flushed mid-artifact and a converter that broke phrases at chunk boundaries. Both are fixed, so the claim is **retired rather than quietly dropped** — the docs now state what replaced it and why.

## Live check first

Before touching the recorded data, eight realistic selections were run through `translateStream` itself against a real qwen3:

- Taiwan vocabulary correct throughout — 網路埠, 資料庫, 記憶體, 預設, 視訊
- a multi-line selection keeps its line breaks (the 2.2.7 flush-point fix, confirmed live)
- no preamble, no echo, no empty output
- an unreachable server still surfaces as the `TypeError` the broker rewrites into the actionable message

items.title: Add Substack blog version and figure PNG exports
Fix train/val leakage, add held-out test eval, add regression tests
items.body:
## Why

The Phase 2 benchmark was measured on a leaking split, so its numbers were not trustworthy. Writing the final report or paper on top of them would have meant citing figures that later had to be retracted.

## Leakage

`build_wheel_dataset.py` shuffled `(image_path, bbox)` pairs at **crop** level and sliced by index, so several vehicles from the same COCO photo landed on both sides of the split — sharing scene, lighting, camera, resolution.

| Class | Leak-prone crops |
|---|---|
| 2-wheeler | 76% |
| 4-wheeler | **91%** |
| 6+ wheeler | 65% |

A second defect: the 3-wheeler class used **whole photos** while every other class used tight crops.

Both fixed — split by source image, and the auto-rickshaw arm now crops from its YOLO labels.

## Corrected benchmark

| Model | Was (leaky) | Now (clean) |
|---|---|---|
| SmallCNN | 0.751 | **0.787** |
| RTMDet-CSPNeXt | 0.683 | **0.695** |
| YOLOv8-cls *(selected)* | 0.867 | **0.861** |

Ranking is unchanged, so the model-selection conclusion is robust. Because both defects changed at once, the deltas are **not** attributable to leakage alone — the report states this.

**A hypothesis I had was disproved:** I suspected 3-wheeler's 0.96 F1 came from the whole-photo shortcut. After cropping it still scores 0.96 — auto-rickshaws are simply distinctive. What actually fell was 4-wheeler (0.81 → 0.70) and 6+ wheeler (0.78 → 0.72); 4-wheeler was the most leak-prone class at 91%, which is the pattern leakage predicts.

## First clean helmet number

mAP@50 **0.764** on the 52-image held-out test split, never previously touched. (0.731 val was used for epoch selection, so it was optimistically biased.) Test > val is small-split variance, not a better model — both corroborate at ~0.73–0.76.

Passenger-helmet classes are weakest on **both** splits (0.545 / 0.565), confirming issue #8 is a real data limitation rather than a split artifact.

## Tests

Adds `tests/` covering every defect that has actually shipped here: inverted compliance, config/weights mismatch, split leakage, and silent DeepSORT/OSNet fallbacks — plus CI. The leakage guard is mutation-tested (fails on an injected leak, passes when clean).

All 7 tests pass.

items.title: Benchmarks: measure the claims, fix the solver they broke
items.body:
The README claimed the Rust core was "faster" and the brief poses research questions 4 and 6 as open. Those were assertions. `benchmarks/run.py` turns them into numbers — and one of the numbers changed the code.

## A measured defect in the default solver

| vars | exact | greedy | annealing | found the optimum? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 0.55ms | 0.11ms | 11.2ms | greedy **+0.236**, annealing exact |
| 12 | 6.9ms | 0.30ms | 17.3ms | both exact |
| 16 | 71.8ms | 0.65ms | 19.8ms | greedy **+0.136**, annealing exact |

`solve()` dispatched to **greedy** above 18 variables — so every production-size selection used the one solver that returns the wrong answer, while the unit tests only ever compared the two on small instances where they happened to agree. Greedy settles into a local minimum and stops.

`solve()` now dispatches to annealing above the exact limit. Selecting the wrong memories quickly is still the wrong answer. A test pins the gap so the reasoning cannot be silently undone; the quality deltas are deterministic and reproduce exactly.

## Research question 4, in one table

Same 24-token budget:

| strategy | picked | tokens | distinct topics |
|---|---|---|---|
| top-k | 3 | 18 | **1** |
| optimised | 3 | 19 | **3** |

Both spend the budget. Top-k spends it on one fact restated three times. The win is not a better ranking — it is refusing to pay twice for the same thing.

## The Rust claim, corrected

**2.3× traversal, 1.3× build** at 400 beliefs. Real, but nothing like the order of magnitude "native core" implies, so the README now says the measured figure and adds that it is not worth installing a toolchain for unless you are hitting that path. I would rather the number be unimpressive and true.

Timings move ±30% between runs, which the README now states rather than presenting one run as definitive. The solver *quality* gaps do not move.

148 tests pass; ruff clean.

items.title: test+build+ci: LCP-array coverage, release profile, and a Rust workflow (independent)
items.body:
**Independent of every other open PR.** Branches from `main`, no behaviour change.

This is #3 reduced to the part @rob-p accepted: the test and build scaffolding, without the packed-key work that PR also carried.

## The crate had no test covering the LCP array

That is the riskiest gap in this codebase. The public entry points discard the LCP array, but the *next* merge level **consumes** it in the three-case decision, so a single wrong entry silently reorders suffixes one level up and the suffix array comes out subtly wrong — permutation intact, order not.

Four tests, checking `lcp[0] == 0` and `lcp[i] == lcp(text[sa[i-1]..], text[sa[i]..])` against a naive oracle over fixtures, random texts across four alphabet sizes, long runs and periodic text, and finite `max_context`.

62 tests before, 66 after.

## The release profile was not what the benchmarks claimed

`bench/README.md` stated the published numbers were taken with `lto = "fat"` and `codegen-units = 1`, supplied by a parent workspace. That workspace is not in this repository. From the commit that made the crate standalone until now, every build made here used `lto = false, codegen-units = 16`, so numbers taken in that window are not comparable with numbers taken since. The profile is pinned here and the stale claim corrected.

In a library crate `[profile.release]` applies only when the crate is the workspace root, so this affects the repo's own tests, examples and benches and is invisible to downstream consumers.

## CI

The repository had no Rust CI, only a docs deploy, while carrying 62 tests with nothing running them.

Runs on `ubuntu-latest` and `macos-latest`, since the LCP kernel and the pooled bucket path are what diverge per platform (x86_64/AVX2 against aarch64/NEON). Tests run in **debug as well as release** — that is not ceremony: debug is what exercises the `debug_assert`s guarding the buffer-length invariants, and on a later branch it caught a `u64` shift-by-64 that release masks to zero and silently gets right. Plus fmt, Clippy with warnings denied, an MSRV check against the declared 1.89, and rustdoc with broken links denied.

The workflow triggers on every branch rather than only `main`. A pull request opened from a fork by a first-time contributor does not run workflows until a maintainer approves them, which is why the API showed no check runs at the tips reviewed in #7; building on push lets the fork produce evidence that can be linked.

## Also

Fixes a pre-existing broken intra-doc link in `build_ext_mem_for_filter`, which pointed at the private `FilteredSource` and would fail the new rustdoc job.

## Review notes from #7, addressed

You asked to correct the stale statement that ruSTAR has not migrated to `SegmentedText` and to clarify that the verifier is for complete plain SAs — both of those live in the packed-key part of #3 and are not in this PR. `verify_sa` is not here either; it belongs with the work that needed it.

items.title: feat: add Opus 5 across pricing data, tools, guides, and site
items.body:
Opus 5 went GA on 2026-07-24 at $5/$25 per 1M input/output, identical to Opus 4.8. The posted rates do not move, so the interesting part is not the number but the shape of the bill: adaptive thinking is on by default and reasoning tokens bill as output at $25/1M, which makes the old "assume 500 output tokens per turn" figure a floor rather than an average.

## What changed

**Pricing data.** `CLAUDE.md` is the source of truth and now carries an Opus 5 entry with the full spec (1M context, 128K max output, 300K on Batch via beta, cache tiers, effort defaults, retirement dates). Opus 4.8 is demoted to legacy but kept as a real option, since it is still the right pin if prompts are tuned to it or if you need thinking off at `xhigh`/`max`. Everything downstream was reconciled against it: all 12 guides, `cheatsheet.md`, `README.md`, `benchmarks/`, `templates/`, both `SKILL.md` copies, `site/src/utils/pricing.ts`, and the pricing tables in all five CLI tools plus their sibling READMEs.

**The `opus` alias now points at Opus 5.** Every tool gained an explicit `opus-4.8` (or `opus_4_8`) key alongside it, so pinning an older model is still priceable rather than silently falling through to a default.

**Minimum cacheable prompt length is now first-class in code, not just prose.** A `cache_control` block on a prefix below the model's floor is silently ignored: no error, no `cache_creation_input_tokens`, and full input price on every turn. The floors span 512 (Opus 5, Fable 5) to 4,096 (Haiku 4.5, Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.5), so a CLAUDE.md that caches fine on Opus quietly pays full price on Haiku. The MCP server and the VS Code extension now warn when a file falls below the floor for the selected model.

**Fast Mode economics rewritten.** It is Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 only now, both at a flat 2x ($10/$50). The 6x tier ($30/$150) no longer exists, so every derived figure that stacked on it was recomputed. The two failure modes are worth knowing apart: Opus 4.7 errors on `speed: "fast"`, while Opus 4.6 silently runs at standard speed and reports `usage.speed: "standard"`.

**Bash tool overhead corrected.** `CLAUDE.md` said +245 tokens and guide 07 said +325/+244. They disagreed, so rather than pick one I checked the live Anthropic docs: it is +325 on Opus 5 / 4.8 / 4.7 and +244 on Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 and earlier. Guide 07 was right; `CLAUDE.md` is now fixed.

**Also:** Sonnet 5 rows with the $2/$10 intro rate through 2026-08-31 (tables use standard $3/$15 so projections stay valid past that date), Mythos Preview / Sonnet 4 / Opus 4 moved to retired, `usage-analyzer` learned to detect `opus-5` and `opus-4.8` session strings, `hooks/cost-logger.sh` now picks its rate from the model instead of hardcoding one, diagrams rebuilt, and plugin manifests bumped to 1.11.0.

## Benchmarks were not relabelled

Measured numbers in `benchmarks/` stay attributed to the model that actually produced them. The summary matrix header previously read `Sonnet 4.6 | Opus 4.8` over columns that were measured on Opus 4.6; that misattribution is corrected to `Sonnet (4.6 measured) | Opus (4.6 measured)` rather than pushed forward another version.

## Verification

- `tools/mcp-cost-server`: `tsc` clean, plus a live JSON-RPC `session_estimate` on model `opus` returning $0.5602 with the Opus 5 adaptive-thinking recommendation firing
- `tools/token-estimator --json`: confirms `opus = Opus 5`, `opus_4_8 = Opus 4.8 (legacy)`
- `claude-rate` and `usage-analyzer` run clean
- `site`: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `pnpm build` succeeds
- `hooks/cost-logger.sh`: `bc` is not installed in my environment, so the script falls back to a flat $0.01 as it did before this change. I validated the `case` rate routing separately rather than claim an end-to-end run: opus-5 and opus-4-8 map to $5/$25, haiku to $1/$5, sonnet-5 to $3/$15, fable-5 and mythos-5 to $10/$50, unknown input to $5/$25.

items.body:
## What & why

Independent, low-risk fixes surfaced by a whole-repository code-review audit, bundled into one PR (to avoid repeated rebases against the in-flight `src/core.ts` PRs). The larger / design-dependent findings from the same audit are filed as their own issues (#126–#135, #138–#141).

**1. Reject two spec-invalid directives** — Closes #124, Closes #125.
- A **repeated `%TAG` for the same handle** used to be silently accepted (last-wins); it now errors, per [YAML 1.2.2 §6.8.2](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#682-tag-directives) (Example 6.17):
  ```yaml
  %TAG ! !foo
  %TAG ! !foo
  ---
  bar
  ```
- A **`%YAML` directive with a higher major version** (e.g. `%YAML 2.0`) used to parse silently; it's now rejected, per [YAML 1.2.2 §6.8.1](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#681-yaml-directives). A higher *minor* (`1.3`) and `%YAML 1.1`/`1.2` are unaffected.
- Both match `js-yaml`; the yaml-test-suite score is unchanged (364/373). Recorded in README's "Decisions and deviations" as intentional strictness over the lenient `yaml` library.

**2. Cap the key-intern cache to bound peak memory** — Closes #136.
- `keyCache` had no size limit (its sibling caches do), so an all-distinct-key document (e.g. a UUID/hostname/timestamp lookup table) grew it unbounded. It's now capped by **cumulative key size (4 MB default)**, and the cap is exposed as an opt-in `optimizations.keyCacheMaxKb` on `parse`/`parseAll`. Parsed output is byte-for-byte unchanged; the `./yaml`/`./js-yaml` compat shims are untouched.

**3. Show the README benchmark table as ratios** — Closes #137.
- The hero table's absolute ms/MB drift with the benchmark box (the old numbers were stale, but the apparent "regression" was a CI-runner baseline shift — `JSON.parse`'s own numbers moved the same way, not a lightning-yaml regression). It now shows **ratios to `JSON.parse`** — parse ~2.1×, peak-RSS ~1.4× for lightning-yaml — which don't swing with the machine, sourced from the newest [`benchmark-data`](https://github.com/jbsiddall/lightning-yaml/tree/benchmark-data) run (commit `4ca6140`, 2026-07-23) with a visible provenance line. The stale "3–5× faster" speed claim was corrected too.

## Correctness gate

- [x] `pnpm typecheck` · `pnpm test` (59/59)
- [x] `pnpm test:unit` (440/440, incl. new directive + key-cache tests) · `pnpm test:stringify` (218/218)
- [x] `pnpm test:suite` — **364/373 (97.6%), unchanged** · `pnpm test:compat` — unchanged
- [x] `pnpm bench:self` — no regression (the key-cache byte-counter is O(1)/key; directive checks are cold-path)

## Code review

- [x] `/code-review` passed — **all eight reviewers approved at commit `fe6999cb87da`**. Pushing new commits invalidates this: re-run `/code-review` and update the hash until all reviewers approve the new HEAD.

Deferred non-blocking notes (would reset the unanimous sign-off for cosmetic gain): the `parse`/`parseAll` per-call option apply/restore is duplicated (tracked in #141), and a `dumpKeyCache` comment still says "mirror" though the two caps now use different strategies — both can ride the #141 cleanup.

## Changeset

- [x] Two changesets, both **minor** for `lightning-yaml`: `reject-malformed-directives` (the two new directive errors) and `cap-key-cache-memory` (adds the public `keyCacheMaxKb` option). The README change is docs-only.

## Correctness note

The two directive changes are the only parse-behavior changes, both spec-backed:
- Duplicate `%TAG` per handle — [§6.8.2](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#682-tag-directives): "It is an error to specify more than one `TAG` directive for the same handle in the same document." (`js-yaml` throws; the `yaml` oracle accepts, but per CLAUDE.md the spec adjudicates over the oracle — recorded as a sanctioned strictness in README.)
- Higher-major `%YAML` — [§6.8.1](https://yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/#681-yaml-directives): a higher major version "should be rejected with an appropriate error message." Only `major ≠ 1` is rejected.

The key-cache cap and README rework change no parse/dump behavior.

items.title: 🪺 docs: close the 2026-08 audit coverage gaps
items.body:
Closes nidus-132.

Eleven documentation coverage gaps left over from the 2026-08 audit (PR #129 landed the
surgical correctness fixes and the em dash sweep). Every claim was re-derived from `src/`,
`sdks/`, and `charts/` rather than trusted, because nothing in CI diffs docs prose against
the route table, the CLI flag surface, the SDK method surface, or the env vars: `docs.yml`
only builds Astro.

## What landed

- **`reference/cli.md`** (new page, + sidebar entry): all 23 subcommands with every flag,
  each flag's `NIDUS_*` binding, and the feature gating that matters (a `--features cli`
  build has no `--embed-*`/`--summarize-*`/`mcp`/`remember`/`recall`; the binstall binary,
  built `--features serve`, has them all).
- **`reference/http-api.md`**: `POST /remember` and `/recall` (`ttl_seconds`,
  `dedupe_threshold`, the redirected id on a dedupe match) plus the `/mcp` mount.
- **`sdks/javascript.md`**: rewritten against the real client (remember/recall,
  `batchSearch` + fuse, `aggregate`, the full options surface, `v.float`/`v.datetime`).
- **`sdks/python.md`** + **`sdks/go.md`**: the Go `Remember` example now compiles against
  `(RememberResult, error)`; `batch_search`/`aggregate` and remember's ttl/dedupe added.
- **`reference/api.md`**: the missing public types, including the backend traits that
  `storage-backends.md` and `memory-stores.md` already promised were documented here.
- **`guides/kubernetes.md`**: the three replica topologies and the Ingress/TLS example
  `http-server.md` pointed at.
- **`guides/http-server.md`**: the `NIDUS_*` table completed from 18 to all 48, grouped by
  family, plus a text-native-ingest section with its failure modes.
- **`index.mdx`**: the server, MCP, and SDKs are now reachable from the front door.
- **`guides/remember-and-recall.md`**: a memory-parity matrix across Rust/HTTP/MCP/CLI.
- **`guides/how-it-works.md`**: the index-cache lifecycle.
- **`reference/performance.md`**: `persist_index` documented as manual, plus measured
  FTS/hybrid/`rank_by` numbers from three new benchmarks.

## Three corrections to the epic body

The ticket was stale against the tree, so the pages follow source, not the ticket:

| nidus-132 said | Tree says |
|---|---|
| 18 CLI subcommands | 23 |
| ~45 `NIDUS_*` vars | 46 clap-declared plus 2 read in `src/diag.rs` |
| `/ready`, `/cluster`, `/refresh`, `/metrics` untyped in the SDKs | only `/metrics`, deliberately |

## Benchmarks

`bench_text_search`, `bench_hybrid` (sweeping `candidates`) and `bench_rank_by` (a
with/without delta, single-threaded) in `benchmarks/benches/nidus_regression.rs`. The
published numbers were measured on an idle machine, not taken from the agent run that
produced the code. Reproduce with a single regex filter, since criterion's harness takes
only one positional argument:

```
cargo bench -p nidus-bench --bench nidus_regression -- 'text_search|hybrid|rank_by'
```

## No version bump

`laws.mjs` `BEHAVIOURAL` covers `^src/`, `^sdks/`, `^Cargo.toml$`, `^Dockerfile$`,
`^install.sh$`. This change touches only `docs/` and `benchmarks/`. Docs deploy through
`docs.yml` independently of `release.yml`, and benchmarks are never published, so a bump
would cut a release containing no shipped code change. `nidus-check laws` reports 0 errors.

## Verification

`just docs-build` green (24 pages), `nidus-check laws` 0 errors, `cargo fmt --check` and
`clippy -p nidus-bench --all-targets -D warnings` clean, the three new benches run to
completion.

`/nidus review` confirmed three factual-drift defects, all fixed and re-verified against
source before this push: `cli.md` called the `--max-concurrent-requests` default unbounded
when `resolve_concurrency(0)` returns `8x` cores floored at 64; six JS examples passed a
bare `Predicate` where `Filter = Predicate[]` is required, so they would not compile; and
the `recall --min-score` rows said "at or below" when the kernel compares `score < min` and
keeps ties.

Two further defects found during the merge, neither of which any CI job would catch: stale
prose in `remember-and-recall.md` claiming `Summarize` stores the original under
`nidus.source` (it stamps `nidus.summary` and `nidus.text`), contradicting the new parity
matrix on the same page; and a wrong ticket citation crediting the `nidus.source` change to
nidus-131 rather than nidus-133.

Filed separately as **nidus-l8k**: the same "at or below" wording is wrong in `src/` too,
at `src/memory.rs:86` and `src/cli/mod.rs:981`, so `nidus recall --help` currently
contradicts the corrected reference page. Left out of this PR because it touches `src/`,
which would pull a version bump into a docs-only change.
