items.title: perf: linear wiring and faster cached resolution, with a benchmark suite to prove it
items.body:
Adds a runtime benchmark suite, then uses it to make the container substantially faster. The two are in one PR because the second half is only trustworthy given the first — and because building the harness immediately exposed two ways it was lying.

## Results

Measured with `pnpm bench` (added here), before vs. after, on the same machine:

| benchmark | before | after | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `add` chain of 200 | 2,158 hz | 21,433 hz | **9.9× faster** |
| `add` chain of 100 | 9,062 hz | 47,210 hz | 5.2× |
| `compose` 20 pre-built modules | 13,859 hz | 32,547 hz | 2.4× |
| cached `get()` — 100 deps | 33,389 hz | 88,979 hz | **2.7× faster** |
| cached `get()` — 3 deps | 65,759 hz | 88,612 hz | 1.35× |
| property access | 43,629 hz | 55,076 hz | 1.26× |
| `clone` a 200-dep container | 43,794 hz | 34,561 hz | **0.79× — slower** |

## The main change

`add` rebuilt the entire resolver map on every call (`{ ...this.resolvers, [name]: resolver }`), making a chain O(N²) at runtime for the same reason it is O(N²) to type-check. `merge` did the same once per merged container. Both now write in place.

That is only safe because of an invariant the code did not previously enforce: **`clone()` handed the clone its source's actual map object**, and the two stayed independent only because every write happened to allocate a replacement. `setResolvers` now copies, and three new tests in `clone.test.ts` pin it in both directions — they fail without the copy.

Smaller wins, all measured:

- `get()` no longer reads the resolved-value cache twice. Worth roughly 2× on a large container, where the map is in V8's dictionary mode and each read is a hash lookup.
- The context `Proxy` no longer calls `.toString()` on every dependency a factory destructures. Symbols now pass through as symbols rather than being looked up under their description.
- The copies in `setResolvers` are entry-by-entry loops rather than spreads — measured 2.4× cheaper for a dictionary-mode map, which is what took `clone` from 0.39× back to 0.79×.

### The `clone` regression is deliberate

It is the irreducible cost of the extra map copy that makes in-place `add` safe: 59 µs → 29 µs to clone a 200-dependency container, a rare operation, in exchange for wins on `add` and `get`, which every consumer pays on every use. Flagging it rather than burying it.

## Two harness bugs found while building the benchmarks

Both were making the numbers lie, and the first predates this PR.

**1. Vitest was running every suite twice.** `tsc` compiles the tests alongside the sources, and Vitest 4 dropped `**/dist/**` from its default excludes — so each suite ran once from `src/` and again from whatever the last build emitted into `dist/`. That is why `pnpm test` reported 16 files for 8. It also means a stale `dist/` could pass a suite the sources fail. Fixed with a `vitest.config.ts`.

**2. The cached-resolution benchmarks were measuring V8's optimiser.** Resolving one fixed name in a batch leaves the call loop-invariant, and V8 hoists it clean out of the loop — in the old build but not the new one. That artefact reported the 2.7× `get()` speedup above as a *1.6× regression*, reproducibly, in both directions. The rows now vary the name per iteration.

The corrected direction was confirmed independently of Vitest, in isolated processes against both compiled builds: 25 ns → 6 ns per cached `get()` at 100 dependencies, stable across alternating runs.

## Notes for review

- No public API or type changes; `dist/` output is unchanged in shape.
- Zero runtime dependencies preserved; the benchmark suite is dev-only and excluded from the published package by the existing `files` rule.
- `pnpm build`, `pnpm test`, `pnpm lint` and `pnpm bench:types` all pass; type-instantiation budgets are unmoved.
- Benchmarks are deliberately **not** wired into CI — wall clock does not transfer between machines, which is the same reasoning `docs/type-benchmarks.md` already gives for gating the type budgets on instantiations instead of time.

items.title: Add lightning, coder-next, deepseek profiles; pin image and re-baseline the fleet
items.body:
Adds three llama.cpp/Vulkan profiles, then — because benchmarking them exposed that the existing numbers were unreliable — pins the toolbox image and re-measures every profile. 12 commits, each independently revertable.

**All figures here were measured on hardware** (gfx1151, llama.cpp build 10400, `llama-bench` r=2 or 3-run cold-prefill probes). Nothing is estimated.

---

## Part 1 — Three new profiles

| Profile | Model | Size | Decode | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lightning` | NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B | ~35 GB | **56.2** | Q8_0, 262K ctx, `parallel_slots: 2` |
| `coder-next` | Qwen3-Coder-Next-80B-A3B | ~85 GB | **42.7 / 38.1 @32K** | Q8_0, non-thinking, big-coder challenger |
| `deepseek` | DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 | ~104 GB | **13.1** | 284B MoE, experimental |

### Spec corrections found during implementation

- **`unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-Next-80B-A3B-GGUF` does not exist** — the published repo is `unsloth/Qwen3-Coder-Next-GGUF`, no size suffix.
- **DeepSeek's `UD-Q3_K_XL` is 128.2 GB, not ~103** — that's ~119 GiB against 125 GiB total, so it cannot load. The "~103 GB" figure matches `UD-IQ3_XXS` (104.2 GB), which is what the profile uses. Pinned by a molecule assertion that rejects `UD-Q3_K_XL`.

### deepseek was gated, then ungated — the gate rationale was wrong

Shipped gated on the reasoning that a code search finds the DSv4 ops (`LIGHTNING_INDEXER`, `DSV4_HC_*`) in `ggml-metal`/`ggml-sycl` but not `ggml-vulkan`, so it "cannot run." **That inference was wrong.** On build 10400 it loads all four shards at ~103 GiB and generates coherent output at the full `-c 131072`. Gate removed; the mechanism stays in the role (it works, and was verified to fire) with no subject.

13.1 tok/s is low for 13B active at IQ3 — bandwidth suggests ~33 — which is *consistent with* partial CPU fallback, but that's inference, not measurement.

---

## Part 2 — The image tag was moving underneath us

`kyuz0/amd-strix-halo-toolboxes:vulkan-radv` is repushed upstream, **twice on 2026-08-13 alone** (02:35 and 05:56 — the second between a pull and a benchmark). A silent move cost `coder-next` **~33% of its decode** at default batch settings: no error, no log line, just slower.

**Pinned to `sha256:41f76c4c…` == build 10400**, with a re-pin procedure that requires re-benchmarking.

## Part 3 — Fleet re-baseline: four published figures were wrong

| profile | documented | measured | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| `coder` | 83.4 | **96.6** | +16% |
| `fast` | 59.4 | **62.1** | +5% |
| `nemotron` | ~95 | **71.1** | **−25%** |
| `lightning` | 51.4 | **56.2** | +9% |
| `super` | 15.6 | **18.8** | +20% |
| `big` | 22.8 | **23.3** | +2% |

**`nemotron`'s `~95` was never measured** — an estimate from the same commit as the `super` `~22` figure corrected in #4. It also invalidated the `lightning` Q8-vs-Q4 analysis, which was anchored on it; the real quant penalty is 21%, not ~50%.

## Part 4 — Batch/ubatch, and why it can't be set fleet-wide

`-ub 2048` beat the default on all six mainstream profiles (+8% to +44% prefill, decode unchanged), so `llamacpp_ubatch_size: 2048` / `llamacpp_batch_size: 4096` are now globals.

**But the optimum is architecture-dependent:**

| Architecture | Best `-ub` | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `qwen3moe` / `qwen35moe` / `nemotron_h_moe` | **2048** | +8% to +44% |
| `bailingmoe3` (Ling-3.0-flash) | **512** (default) | 2048 costs ~18% |
| `deepseek4` | **1024** | 2048 costs **22%** |

Both novel architectures reject what every mainstream one prefers. `deepseek` pins `ubatch_size: 1024` accordingly.

**Trap worth knowing:** llama.cpp clamps the micro-batch to the logical batch, so `-b 512 -ub 2048` silently does nothing. That made coder-next's first tuning attempt a no-op.

## Part 5 — Corrections to this PR's own earlier claims

- **coder-next's "−35% decode falloff" was not architectural.** Build-matched at 10400 it's **−11%**. The original came from build 8985 at default batch — toolchain and config, not attention design.
- **Context comparison overstated 2×** (Codex catch). `parallel_slots: 2` means each request gets 131072, not 262144. Split into per-request and aggregate rows.
- **`nerdsrun-os-chunks.md` removed** (Codex catch) — swept in by `git add -A`, now gitignored.

---

## Testing

`mise run lint` and `mise run test` pass; CI green.

- **Guard verified to fire**: gated profile stops after resolving 22 tasks; control completes `failed=0`
- **`-np` doesn't double-render**: `parallel_slots` only emits when defined, so profiles passing `-np 1` via `extra_args` are untouched
- **`parallel_slots` semantics confirmed live**: `n_slots = 2, n_ctx_slot = 131072`
- Molecule pins deepseek's quant (rejecting `UD-Q3_K_XL`), its KV defaults, and asserts no profile is gated
- Quadlet render test (from #4) covers all three new profiles automatically

## Not measured

- Quality/agentic evaluation is **not part of this PR** — it lives in `~/ling-expedition/` on the host. Summary: `coder-next` and DeepSeek both score 6/6 multi-turn and 32/32 tool-call validity; they diverge on error recovery (DeepSeek 6/6, coder-next 3/6 — it fabricates and reports success when blocked).
- KV growth at 128K/256K for `super`; MTP throughput A/B.
- `minimax` ubatch never swept (pinned at 1024 from an earlier measurement).

items.title: fix(search): penalized expansion backfill, gated trigram build, dense-channel and build perf fixes
items.body:
WP2b of the 0.3.0 search-pipeline hardening program. References epic #75. Built on top of the in_force/abstain modes (PR #80).

## Findings fixed

**(a) Penalized expansion backfill (main false-positive vector).** Query expansion (synonym #38 + co-occurrence #40) previously folded derived terms into the single FTS5 `MATCH`. FTS5 bm25 has no positional preference, so a doc matching only a synonym received full idf weight and could outrank a doc matching the user's actual term — the "appended = down-weighted" claim in the module docstrings was false. `Index.search` now runs the user's own terms as a PRIMARY `MATCH` and the expansion terms in a SEPARATE penalized backfill pass (`_expansion_backfill`) whose hits can only rank BELOW the worst primary hit. The docstrings in `query_expansion.py` / `cooccurrence.py` are corrected.

**(b) Co-occurrence defaults hardened.** `min_count` 2→3, `min_pmi` 0.0→0.1; added a corpus-size floor (`KB_COOCCURRENCE_MIN_DOCS`, default 50) that auto-disables the table on small corpora where PMI is noise, and a per-doc unique-token cap (`KB_COOCCURRENCE_MAX_DOC_TOKENS`, default 400) bounding the O(n²) pair counting so a multi-thousand-word doc is no longer a build-time memory cliff.

**(c) Gated trigram index.** `fts_trigram` (a full second tokenized copy of the corpus, ~2-3× index-size / build-time tax) is now created and populated ONLY when the trigram fallback is enabled (`KB_TRIGRAM_MODE=on`), not unconditionally. A default deployment pays no trigram cost.

**(d) Rank-class invariant made true.** `SearchHit` gained `rank_class` (`RANK_CLASS_PRIMARY` / `RANK_CLASS_BACKFILL`). The status and hybrid rerankers now sort by `(rank_class, score)`, so a backfill (expansion/trigram) hit can never be reordered above a primary — even when a reranker ADDS status deltas or RE-NORMALISES scores. The previous score-only "strictly worse" floor could be lifted by an active-status boost or the hybrid blend. The trigram module docstring is corrected accordingly.

**(e) Status prior.** Left as the intended quality knob (in_force hard filtering from #80 covers the correctness-critical case). The status reranker is now rank-class-aware and tested; no calibration change was needed to make it sane.

**(f) Dense channel includes intent vocabulary.** The text embedded at build time now includes `applies_when` and `tags` (the curated intent phrases a paraphrase query embeds near), not just title/description/body.

**(g) Vector perf.** The id→vector matrix is loaded from SQLite ONCE per build and cached (keyed by db file (size, mtime), invalidated transparently by the atomic swap). This removes the per-candidate `get_vector` connection the hybrid reranker used to open and the per-query full-table re-read in `dense_candidates`.

**(h) `>limit` bug.** `search()` now truncates to `limit` unconditionally. Previously truncation lived only inside the reranker branch, so with embeddings configured but no reranker set the dense union could return more than `limit` hits.

**(i) Build perf.** `Index.build` runs a single `git log --name-only` pass for every file's last-commit time (one subprocess instead of N) and reads + parses each markdown file exactly once (was three times: two parses plus a separate content read). Per-file `(last_modified, source)` metadata is byte-for-byte identical; the batched pass uses `-z` NUL-delimited output with `core.quotePath=false` so filenames with spaces/unicode round-trip exactly rather than falling back to mtime.

**(j) Malformed frontmatter surfaced.** A doc whose front-matter block is present but is invalid YAML (so its `status`/`supersedes` are silently dropped, quietly disabling staleness protection) is now logged at WARN per doc, counted, and surfaced via `Index.malformed_frontmatter_count` and the `malformed_frontmatter` field in `health()`. A doc with genuinely no front matter is not counted.

## Test evidence

New `tests/test_search_hardening.py` plus updates to `test_trigram.py` / `test_cooccurrence.py`:
- (a) expansion-only hit never outranks a primary (with rank_class assertions).
- (d) status AND hybrid rerankers keep backfill below primaries even with an active-status / perfect-cosine backfill hit.
- (b) corpus floor / threshold behavior; hardened defaults.
- (c) trigram table absent when off, present when on, and off-build strictly smaller than on-build.
- (h) `>limit` regression (embeddings on, no reranker).
- (f) embedded text asserted to include `applies_when` + tags.
- (g) vector matrix loaded ≤1× per query; cache invalidated on rebuild.
- (i) batched git timestamps equal per-file query results; special-char filename resolves via git; non-git KB falls back to mtime.
- (j) malformed-frontmatter counter + health field; no-frontmatter not counted.

Full suite + `ruff` + `mypy` all green. Rebased onto latest `origin/release/0.3.0`; CHANGELOG conflict resolved keeping all entries.

## Peer review (codex)

First pass: **0 Blockers**, 2 Concerns, 2 Nits. All verified points confirmed correct (expansion backfill flow, gated trigram with no code path assuming its existence, `>limit` fix, vector batch fetch removing per-hit connections, no committed benchmark numbers touched). All four items were fixed:
- Concern (git-path exactness): switched to `-z` NUL-delimited + `core.quotePath=false`, no path `.strip()`; added a special-char-filename regression test.
- Concern (hybrid rank-class not directly tested): added a pure hybrid-reranker test (perfect-cosine backfill at weight=1.0 must stay below a weak-cosine primary).
- Nit: corrected the stale `config.py` "trigram always built" comment.
- Nit: strengthened `test_trigram_hits_appended_after_primary` to assert primaries precede backfill via rank_class.

Second pass empirically confirmed the git-parser byte structure matches the implementation. No Blockers at any point.

items.title: Docs: refresh for 256 KiB default and current performance numbers
items.body:
Docs/benchmarks only — no code change. Follow-up to the chunk_size default bump (#13) and read speedups (#12).

## Fixes
- **`docs/performance.md`**
  - *Stale:* "default `chunk_size` is 64KB" → **256 KiB**.
  - *Now-contradictory:* the tip suggested increasing to `128*1024`, which is **below** the new 256 KiB default — reworded to `512*1024`/`1024*1024`, and noted the default already sits at the zlib-offload threshold.
  - Refreshed the benchmark tables from a current run: text bulk ~2.9× (~37 vs ~13 MB/s), binary bulk equivalent (~61 vs ~62 MB/s), JSONL ~1.8×, line iteration ~1.35M/s, concurrency up to ~6× when latency-bound.
  - **Corrected** the small-chunk row: the old table claimed "1.3× faster", but aiogzip is actually ~2× *slower* on 10-byte writes (per-await overhead) — now stated honestly.
- **`README.md`** — reworded the Binary I/O bullet to note fast bulk reads.
- **`benchmarks/README.md`** — listed the two new `bench_io` cases (read-all isolated, text large reads) added in #12.

## Notes
- `mkdocs build --strict` passes; markdownlint clean.
- Benchmark numbers are illustrative (single recent run on one machine); they were never exact and remain approximate.

items.title: Commit benchmark run logs as provenance for the published findings
items.body:
## What

Commits the 40 benchmark **run logs** that were sitting untracked, as provenance for the numbers published across `docs/FINDINGS.md`, `docs/negative-results.md`, and `docs/figures/`.

## Why

`.gitignore` excludes `benchmark/results/*.jsonl`, so the per-item outcomes behind every published number are **absent from a fresh clone**. These stdout logs are the only committed artifact showing the runs actually happened — each carries its loaded item count, per-item verdicts, drop warnings, and the final `RESULTS` line.

That closes a real gap noted in `docs/figures/README.md`: a reader could already verify our claims ledger against our prose (`verify_ledger()` greps every numeric cell for its literal value in the doc it cites — 99 numbers), but had **nothing to confirm the underlying runs occurred at all**.

## Why these files, and why now

`.gitignore` excludes only `*.jsonl`, never `*.log`, and **8 log files were already tracked** (`baseline_mmlu_pro_stem_seed42.log`, `lever_baseline_seed123.log`, and others). This makes the set consistent rather than arbitrarily partial. 40 files, ~2.9 MB.

## Specifically useful for auditing the caveats we publish

The logs are most valuable where they document our own failures:

| Log | What it evidences |
|---|---|
| `aime_cheap_pilot_seed42.log` | The **32/60 panel + 12/60 baseline drops** that invalidated that run — the survivorship evidence is now *in* the repo, not merely described in it |
| `lever_chem_thinking_gate_seed{314,217,471}.log` | The per-seed chemistry drops behind the "band wider than the point estimate" caveat |
| `lever_qwen38_panel_supergpqa_seed42.log` | The ~30% timeout drops that make its 87.3% a survivor-set artifact |
| `qwen38_baseline_seed123.log` | The 73/78 run behind the 93.6% family-best bar that `negative-results.md` flags as **upper-biased, not settled** |
| `moo_m1_eval.log` | The single eval behind the MoO router table |

## Reviewer notes

- **This PR does not contain the session's main work.** The figures, findings docs, negative-results catalogue, claims ledger, IFEval/SimpleQA harnesses and lever builds were all committed directly to `main` earlier and are already merged. This branch carries only the log provenance.
- **Deliberately excluded**, both left uncommitted on purpose:
  - `.claude/scheduled_tasks.lock` — machine-local scheduler state that churns every session.
  - `site_data/cases.json` — a pre-existing uncommitted change that predates this session and feeds the live public site, which stays untouched while Devpost judging is open (additive-only posture).
- **No code, no test, and no published number changes.** Log files only; the offline suite is unaffected (711 passing on `main`).

items.title: perf: coalesce Canvas.String() per-cell styling into per-run calls
items.body:
## Update — rebased on #363's review fixes + corrected live-CPU methodology

**Rebased** onto `fix/363-disk-raster-memo` after its pre-merge review
fixes landed (`abe8390` — self-healing cache hit path, off-canvas skip,
LRU-bounded offset cache, `systemIdx` in the cache key; see PR #365).
No changes were needed to this PR's own code — `Canvas.String()`'s
run-length coalescing is independent of those fixes.

**Cheap-hardening follow-ups** added in a new commit
(`a58766a`) after the rebase, both flagged in the same review pass:
- `canvas_test.go`: `TestSetCellLabelColored`'s ANSI assertion is
  tightened from "the foreground open code appears somewhere in the
  output" back to "the open code sits directly against the label
  text" (`openCode+"view:"`), restoring the original assertion's
  strength while staying coalescing-safe.
- `canvas_string_coalesce_test.go`: added
  `TestStringCoalescedMatchesReferenceEveryCellDistinctColor` — the
  worst case for run-length coalescing, a textured disk where every
  pixel gets a different color so no run is ever longer than one
  cell. The existing tests all use long same-color runs (a filled
  disk); a run-boundary bookkeeping bug could hide behind those.

**Corrected live-CPU methodology (important — see PR #365 for the
full writeup):** the live idle-CPU numbers originally reported below
were each measured by launching one binary at a time in its own
session and comparing against a number from an earlier, separate
session — which turned out to be unreliable on this machine (ambient
CPU availability drifts noticeably between sessions). Re-measured with
`main`, `363-only`, and `363+364` running **simultaneously**, sampled
interleaved with `ps -o %cpu` so every sample reflects identical
system conditions for all three (30 samples, 2 rounds × 15):

```
main:              22.65% avg
363-only:          19.19% avg   (-15.3% relative to main)
363+364 (this PR): 18.36% avg   (-19.0% relative to main;
                                 -4.3% relative to 363-only)
```

So **this PR's own marginal contribution on top of #363 is small**
(~4.3% relative, not the "~20.3% → ~12.6%" originally claimed) — the
`pprof` finding that `Canvas.String()`'s share of `Render()`'s own
cost dropped substantially (~20% → ~11% cum) is still accurate, but
`Render()` itself is only a fraction of the process's total per-tick
cost (tmux/pty I/O, Bubble Tea's own diff/render pipeline, goroutine
scheduling, GC), which bounds how much a `Render()`-only fix can move
the live number. The fix is still correct and worth keeping (it's a
real, measured, allocation-reducing change with a full regression-test
suite proving byte-for-byte output equivalence), but the live-CPU win
should be read as modest, not dramatic.

The benchmark numbers below (`BenchmarkOrbitViewRenderIdle`,
`go tool pprof`) are unaffected by this — they were measured with
controlled, single-process methodologies that don't have the
cross-session drift confound. Only the **live `ps -o %cpu`
comparison** needed correcting.

`go vet ./...` and `go test ./... -race -count=1` remain green on the
rebased branch, re-verified (including 3× repeated runs of
`tui/screens` + `tui/widgets` to rule out test-ordering flakes).

---

## Summary

Measure-first follow-on to #363 (stacked on that branch — this PR's
diff is `canvas.go`/`canvas_test.go` only).

## Fresh profile after #363

`go test -cpuprofile` on `BenchmarkOrbitViewRenderIdle` (added in
#363) named the new dominant idle cost: `Canvas.String()` — 20.16%
cumulative of `Render()`'s own cost — almost entirely inside one line
(`go tool pprof -list` attributed 490ms of `Canvas.String()`'s 1.29s
total to it):

```go
b.WriteString(lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(fg).Render(string(ch)))
```

This ran once per **colored cell**, invoking the full
`lipgloss.Style.Render()` pipeline (tab conversion, word-wrap, border,
alignment, grapheme-cluster width scanning via `uniseg`/`ansi`) for
every single glyph — even though a filled body disk (the exact thing
#363 just made cheap to *rasterize*) is mostly long horizontal runs of
the identical color. This is precisely the "lipgloss style rendering
and uniseg/ansi string-width scanning" cost the issue predicted.

## Fix

`String()` now coalesces each row into runs of consecutive,
identically-styled cells (same `(fg, styled)` boundary rule as
before — a space is never "styled," matching the pre-existing `ch !=
' '` exemption) and calls `Style.Render()` once per **run** instead of
once per **cell**. Same characters, same colors, far fewer
`Style.Render()` calls for typical scenes.

## Correctness

`internal/tui/widgets/canvas_string_coalesce_test.go` adds:
- `referenceString()` — the exact pre-#364 per-cell implementation,
  kept side-by-side as ground truth.
- `expandRunsToPerChar()` — un-batches the new coalesced ANSI output
  back into one-escape-pair-per-glyph (the shape the old code always
  produced).
- `TestStringCoalescedMatchesPerCellReference` /
  `...AcrossPalette` assert **byte-for-byte equivalence once
  un-batched**, across multiple colors/radii/gaps/cell-overlays — not
  just "looks the same."

`TestSetCellLabelColored` (`canvas_test.go`) needed a small update: it
asserted a single-glyph-wrapped ANSI substring (`"\x1b[96mv\x1b[0m"`),
which no longer appears literally once adjacent same-colored glyphs
("view:") coalesce into one run. The fix derives just the ANSI *open*
code from a lipgloss sample render and checks for that instead, which
holds regardless of run length. This isn't a re-baseline — the color
behavior the test guards (the label renders in the requested
foreground) is unchanged; only how narrowly the previous assertion was
written needed to change.

## Profile after this fix

Same `BenchmarkOrbitViewRenderIdle`, `go tool pprof -top -cum`:

- `Canvas.String()` cum: 20.16% -> 11.29% of `Render()`'s cost
- `FillTexturedDiskTagged` (the #363 fix) stays flat, ~10-14% run to
  run (benchmark noise)
- Next-largest remaining contributor: orbit-line ellipse sampling
  (`Canvas.DrawEllipseClassTagged` / `flattenEllipse`) — pure
  geometry, not lipgloss/uniseg, out of this issue's "frame-assembly
  churn" scope

## Live idle CPU

Same methodology as #363 (`ps -o %cpu`, warp 1×, default LEO-Earth
start, 120×36 terminal, orbit screen, ~40s settle):

```
after #363 alone:        ~20.3% avg (14.6–22.5% range, 8 samples)
after #363 + this fix:   ~12.6% avg (11.3–14.2% range, 8 samples)
```

Combined with #363: **baseline ~26.0% avg -> ~12.6% avg, a ~52%
relative reduction.** Not literally single digits — the remaining
orbit-line geometry cost is real, measured, and genuinely out of scope
for a lipgloss/uniseg-shaped fix — but the two slices together close
the large majority of the original gap.

Tick rate, physics step, and warp clamps are untouched — this only
touches how an already-computed frame gets turned into a string.

## Test plan

- [x] `go vet ./...` green
- [x] `go test ./... -race -count=1` green
- [x] New regression tests prove byte-for-byte equivalence to the
      pre-fix per-cell rendering once un-batched (see Correctness
      above)
- [x] Spot-checked orbit / maneuver / session screens at the app's
      actual terminal floor (104×24 — `MinTerminalWidth` in
      `sizegate.go`; the app gates below that with a "too small"
      screen rather than rendering, so 80×24 isn't a reachable
      in-game size) and at 160×48: all three render correctly, no
      garbling, same content as before this change
- [x] Tick rate / physics step untouched (no changes outside
      `internal/tui/widgets/canvas*.go`)

Closes #364

items.title: Release 0.15.0: dart-sass JS-API parity fix (breaking), honest benchmarks, Node 24 LTS
items.body:
30 commits. One breaking change, one shipped-bug fix, and a substantial correction to how we measure and publish performance.

## Breaking (npm packages only)

**`result.css` no longer ends with a trailing newline** (`4cbb353f`). grass's JS API was appending one; dart-sass's JS API does not — so every result differed from dart-sass by a single byte. This was a real bug in the shipped npm package, found by a benchmark's byte-equality assertion (the CLI-level parity corpus is structurally incapable of seeing JS-API divergences).

The CLI and the Rust API are **unchanged** — both still end with a newline, matching dart-sass's CLI. dart-sass deliberately has different trailing-newline behavior for its CLI and its JS API; grass now matches both.

Consumers writing `result.css` straight to a file and needing the previous bytes should append `"\n"` themselves. Version bumped **0.14.6 → 0.15.0** (minor, not patch — it is breaking).

## Benchmarks: measured honestly, and several claims came down

The performance numbers on the README were wrong in ways that all flattered us. Fixed:

- **Corpus speed ratios were startup-inflated.** The 14-project corpus timed dart via `npx sass` (npx resolution + Dart VM boot — ~0.7s just to compile a one-line file) against grass as a native binary, producing 12x–134x "speedups". Removed at the generator; the corpus now times both engines **warm and in-process**. Honest result: **2.5x–18.1x, median 6.37x**, all 14 still byte-identical to dart-sass 1.101.0.
- **Peak memory was inflated ~3x.** We compared grass's *native* binary against dart-sass's *pure-JS npm CLI*, which carries an entire Node runtime. Both dart CLIs emit byte-identical CSS — the gap was packaging, not memory. Corrected to a like-for-like native comparison: **3.3x less** (was claiming 8.90x).
- **We were benchmarking a stale dart-sass** (sass-embedded 1.97.3) while claiming parity against 1.101.0. Bumped to the latest; the newer dart-sass narrowed our lead and we published the smaller numbers.
- **We were benchmarking on Node 23** — an odd-numbered, non-LTS release nobody runs in production. Everything re-measured on **Node 24 LTS**; `.nvmrc` pins it.

The README now carries the full 14-project table, WASM figures, and a footnote naming the method for every row.

## CI: Node 20 → 24 LTS

Node 20 reached end of life in April 2026. Every Node reference bumped: `setup-node` pins, the x86_64 Rosetta test's Node tarball (and its SHA-256), and the `node:*-alpine` images used for the musl napi tests. Safe for consumers — `crates/napi` targets `napi4` and N-API is ABI-stable, so the build Node does not constrain the runtime.

Note: Node 22 is still a supported LTS and is now untested. A `[22, 24]` matrix would cover it cheaply; deliberately not done here.

## Also in this release

- Release CLI binaries are now PGO-trained on a multi-project corpus.
- N-API concurrency documented: `compileAsync` parallelizes on the libuv threadpool. Raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` before the first async call — 3.76x at the default pool of 4, 6.63x at 8 (8 concurrent Bootstrap compiles).
- New bench harnesses: `bench/scripts/napi-concurrent.mjs`, `bench/scripts/wasm-compare.mjs` (four-engine, raw byte-equality gate — the one that found the newline bug).

## Gates

sass-spec 13,849/13,888; real-world corpus 14/14 byte-identical to dart-sass 1.101.0; Bootstrap/USWDS byte-zero; `cargo test`, fmt, clippy clean; napi + pkg-publish suites green. CLI output verified byte-identical to `npx sass@1.101.0`.

items.title: feat(sa): v2 .osa2 for all allele-level & positional sources; --format auto default
items.body:
## Summary

Makes the v2 `.osa2` supplementary-annotation format the **smarter default** across every allele-level and positional source, and flips `sa-build --format` to `auto` so users get the best format per source without having to know which is which.

Before this PR, v2 was half-wired (numeric sources only) and opt-in. After it, **13 sources** have a v2 encoder spanning four payload shapes — numeric, categorical, opaque-blob, and positional — each with v1↔v2 parity tests. Only gene-level (`.oga`) and `custom_*` sources remain v1-only, by design.

## What's new

- **`--format auto` (new default):** builds v2 for sources that support it, v1 for the rest. `osa`/`osa2` still force a format. The supported-source list lives in one place (`OSA2_SUPPORTED_SOURCES` / `source_supports_osa2`) feeding both the `auto` dispatch and the `osa2` error message.
- **Numeric v2:** gnomAD, 1000G, TOPMed — packed into parallel u32 columns (AF as a quantized float column, counts exact).
- **AlphaMissense (new source, Zenodo 8208688):** score + 3-level categorical class — the first v2 source to use categorical string tables. First-class in JSON/tab/VCF (`FV_ALPHAMISSENSE`).
- **Whole-record-blob v2:** dbSNP, COSMIC, ClinVar, REVEL, PrimateAI, dbNSFP — stored as one opaque JSON blob per variant (empty-alias `JsonBlob` field the reader emits verbatim), so output is **byte-identical to v1** while v2's chunk-level zstd of the blob column shrinks the DB sharply.
- **Positional v2:** PhyloP, GERP, DANN — a new `var32::positional_key` keys allele-less per-base records by coordinate (the allele-matched Var32 path rejects empty alleles). These **stream** (never buffer — PhyloP is ~3B positions). Largest size win of any source.

## Benchmarks — reproduced for this PR

All numbers below were re-run on this branch; the two examples (`bench_shapes`, `bench_v1_vs_v2`) are deterministic (hash-based synthetic data, no RNG).

**Size, `v2/v1` by payload shape (`bench_shapes`), across scale:**

| shape | 2M | 10M | 20M |
|---|---|---|---|
| numeric (gnomAD-like) | 1.12× | 0.67× | 0.51× |
| score (AlphaMissense-like) | 1.07× | 0.93× | 0.51× |
| id_string (dbSNP-like) | 0.40× | 0.30× | 0.37× |
| array_blob (ClinVar-like) | 0.40× | 0.34× | 0.39× |
| positional (PhyloP-like) | 0.23× | 0.23× | 0.23× |

**Speed + size at genome scale (`bench_v1_vs_v2`, 10M records, strided VCF-like workload):**

| metric | result |
|---|---|
| query throughput | **4.13× v1** (146K → 605K q/s) |
| on-disk size | **0.67×** (33% smaller) |
| build time | 4.50× v1 (one-time) |

v2 wins on size at genome scale (dramatically for blob/positional), and is faster to query on the sparse, scattered lookups a real VCF produces. It is *not* a size win for small inputs (fixed per-chunk/ZIP overhead) — hence `auto`, not always-v2. Every claim in `README.md`, `docs/SUPPLEMENTARY_ANNOTATIONS.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md` was checked against these runs.

## Correctness & review

Full suite: **641 tests pass, 0 failures**; clippy exits clean (no new lint categories vs. master). v1↔v2 parity is verified by test for every v2 source, including positional allele-independence and ClinVar's `is_array` nesting.

Two independent deep reviews (v2 core; pipeline/parity) turned up two substantive items, both fixed in the final commit:

1. **Swallowed final-flush error (medium):** `ZipWriter::finish` returns the inner writer unflushed; a `BufWriter`'s Drop discards flush errors, so a disk-full on the final write could leave a truncated `.osa2` reported as success. Now flushes explicitly so the error propagates and the partial file is cleaned up.
2. **Overstated "identical output" for gnomAD (low-medium):** v2 quantizes AF to a fixed 5e-7 resolution while v1 keeps the raw VCF float. Counts stay exact and every real frequency matches, but the rarest gnomAD v4 singletons (AF ~6e-7) fall below the floor. Docstrings and the (mathematically wrong) `AF_MULTIPLIER` comment corrected; blob sources and AlphaMissense remain genuinely byte-identical.

Two low-severity latent fragilities were noted and deemed non-triggering for real inputs (kept as documented invariants): the whole-record-blob early-return assumes its sole-field schema, and duplicate positional coordinates would resolve nondeterministically (per-base sources are one-record-per-coordinate).

## Notes for reviewers

- Rebased onto current `master`; contains exactly the 10 v2 commits (the earlier shared-branch commits already merged via #65 were dropped).
- No format-version bump needed — existing v1 databases read unchanged; v2 is additive.

items.title: docs: documentation staleness audit — factual fixes + honest RL framing
items.body:
Audit of the documentation set against the live code, config, and the `experiments/` reports, to make the docs a trustworthy base for downstream writing. The per-module internals refresh itself already landed on `main`; this PR is the follow-up audit fixes.

All benchmark numbers (forecasting MAPE, autoscaler SLA, anomaly F1/recall, routing CIs) were checked and found accurate and consistent across docs. The issues were facts and framing.

## Factual fixes (verified, single correct answer)
- **ARIMA artifact order** corrected `(3,0,1)` -> `(2,0,2)` across 8 files (13 spots). Verified by unpickling `services/forecasting/models/arima_model.pkl` (`order=(2,0,2)`, `exog_cols=None`); `(3,0,1)` is the separate, unshipped ARIMAX run. The 25.0% MAPE / 36.9 MB figures are correct and belong to the `(2,0,2)` model.
- **Isolation Forest** status in SOT corrected from "scaffolded / not present" to shipped + selectable (`models/isolation_forest.pkl` exists; `trend_rule` is the deployed default).
- **`max_backends`** `5` -> `3` in the SOT "canonical from config/policy.yaml" constraint and example block, and in the PROJECT_WALKTHROUGH single-file-config example (matches committed `policy.yaml`).
- **lb-sidecar / data-plane**: "(future) T2.1 sidecar" -> shipped; "PPO-driven routing" -> rl-engine-driven (deployed policy is `monotone`, PPO shadow-only).
- **`smartload.scale` envelope** `ScaleEvent` -> `ScalingEvent` (matches `services/shared/contracts.py`).
- **SOT version header** `1.0.7bp` -> `1.0.7bq`.

## Framing fixes
- **Routing-plane overclaim** reconciled to the audited reality already in the module docs: the deployed router is the non-learned latency-monotone capacity-aware `candidate_mono`; the trained PPO bandit is round-robin-equivalent and shadow-only. Updated SOT section 8.7 Purpose and the N2.4 acceptance row (keeps the original spec gate, records the honest outcome), and the README tagline / intro / routing bullet.
- **README datasets table** rewritten to the datasets the shipped benchmarks and training actually use: Azure Functions Trace 2019, FIFA World Cup 1998, Alibaba Cluster Trace 2018 (forecasting/autoscaler evaluation), Server Machine Dataset (SMD / OmniAnomaly, Isolation-Forest training; fixes the prior "Yahoo SMD" misattribution), and the in-repo synthetic profiles. Dropped Google Borg and NAB, which no shipped benchmark uses.

## Code
- One comment-only fix in `services/rl-engine/obs_builder.py`: `N_MAX_BACKENDS` must be `>=` `policy.yaml` `max_backends` (absent slots are zero-padded), not equal; notes the current value of 3. No behaviour change.

items.title: docs: apply advisor review to model survey (session 69)
items.body:
## Summary

Applies the advisor's 8 recommended edits to `docs/findings/model-updates-2026-05.md` (session 68 model survey), plus cascading updates to memory and tracking files.

**Core theme:** The advisor identified that benchmark numbers and Ollama tag claims were sourced from secondary blogs, not primary sources. The risk is treating unverified blog claims as engineering commitments (persona migrations, DECISIONS.md edits, models.yaml deprecations). These changes invert the order: verify locally first, commit to swaps second.

## Changes in `docs/findings/model-updates-2026-05.md`

1. **Methodology footnote at top** — warns that many existence/benchmark claims come from secondary sources; points to `ollama.com/library/<tag>` for verification
2. **TL;DR re-framed** — "P0 — Swap" → "P0 — Pull + Benchmark" and "P0 — Pull + Probe"; swap/probe explicitly conditional on local validation

4. **Qwen3.7 Max qualified** — single-source origin flagged; unusual naming convention noted; verify from official Qwen blog before acting
5. **Benchmark numbers footnoted** — ~88%/~62% (qwen3.6-coder) and ~85%/~55% (qwen2.5-coder) marked as secondary-source claims with ¹ notation; footnote notes the official Qwen2.5-Coder report had ~90% — if baseline is wrong, the delta is artificially narrowed

7. **Llama 4 Scout 10M context qualified** — effective useful range for RAG ~200K–1M, not 10M; still a step change over current 128K ceiling
8. **Independent benchmark Y/N column** — added to all 3 frontier-distilled tables; ✅ Yes for DeepSeek-R1 (official paper); ❌ No for all Jackrong and TeichAI community models
9. **Changes-made response section** — added at doc bottom with table mapping each advisor point to the change applied

## Cascading Updates

| File | Change |
|---|---|

items.title: fix: dictation, engine lifecycle, and insights defects
items.body:
Follow-up fixes from the review of #17 / #18, against `dev`. Both of those are merged, so nothing here is a merge gate for them. **Every finding in the review is now addressed.**

## Dictation defects

**Alt+Shift+F9 could never be saved.** The id was in both the picker and `legacyShortcutIds`, and the load path rewrites every legacy id to the default, so it silently reset on each launch. The migration test looped over that constant and asserted each maps to the default, meaning the suite *enforced* the bug; it now iterates an explicit retired list, and a new test walks the picker so any option that cannot round-trip fails the suite.

**A one-key custom shortcut could take over the keyboard.** Recording had no minimum and no modifier requirement, so a single letter became the global hold shortcut, with no way to type out of it. A capture now needs two keys including a modifier, and OS-owned combinations are refused. The save also awaits re-registration, which previously reported success while the old shortcut was still live.

**A release beating the press left a recorder nobody owned.** `startListening` set the phase and recorder synchronously, then suspended before `recorder.start()`; a stop in that window stopped a recorder that had not begun, and the suspended start then opened one nothing would close — on Android, a live mic after the user let go. The desktop registrars shielded the global shortcut, but the Dictate mic tile and the accessibility service did not, so the invariant now lives in `DictationController`. The test asserts call order and fails against the previous controller.

## Speech engine

**The model's native memory survived a language switch.** `shutdown()` killed the isolate on the line after sending the request, usually preempting `recognizer.free()` — the exact thing the RAM policy exists to prevent. The worker now acknowledges *after* freeing, shutdown waits for that, and the kill is a five-second backstop.

**A dead worker hung every later dictation.** `transcribe()` awaited its reply with no death port, so a worker lost mid-decode left the future pending forever while `isReady()` still returned true and `prepare()` early-returned — broken until restart. The death signal now lives as long as the isolate, and the handles are dropped so the next prepare respawns.

## Insights

Streaks and the activity grid used `Duration(days:)` on local dates. Across a DST boundary that lands on 23:00 the previous day, so streaks reset and every grid cell read as empty. Now calendar arithmetic. The page also passed failed dictations to the stats, which deflated words-per-session and let a day of nothing but failures extend the streak; it passes `successfulEntries`.

The DST tests were verified the honest way: they **fail on the old code and pass on the new under `TZ=America/New_York`** in WSL, since they cannot fail in India's timezone — which is why this was invisible locally.

## Storage and downloads

Failure audio in `recordings/failed/` was never swept, so a WAV whose history entry vanished stayed forever, against the promise that a recording dies with its entry. It is now age-swept at the same 30-day bound, leaving recent (still retryable) audio alone.

A paused download was polled as live but nothing ever resumed one, so it spun every 500 ms forever with a frozen progress bar. It now resumes once, and falls back to a fresh download if that is refused.

## Benchmark numbers

The corpus grew after the shipped figures were written, and the two models had been measured on different corpora. Both re-measured on the same 101 clips:

| | parakeet-unified (shipped) | Parakeet v3 (previous) |
|---|---|---|
| Overall | **4.4%** (129/2945) | 9.0% (265/2945) |
| Indian English | **7.0%** (31/443) | 11.7% (52/443) |
| US English | **4.8%** (18/372) | 11.6% (43/372) |

This removes the review's caveat: the two sides are now the same audio, and the result is better than the old text claimed.

## Documentation

Corrected where it no longer matched the code: `_isIntact` checks size only (and why re-hashing 654 MB per launch buys nothing), `resumeFromBytes` is a hint the production downloader ignores, the noise-suppression toggle is no longer gated on a desktop helper binary, and `prompt` is a seam every shipped language passes null for. `TYPEMATE_GGML_NO_FREE` claimed benchmark tools set it — nothing *can*, since Dart cannot mutate its own environment — so it now documents the shell form and points at the Release DLL.

## Test organisation (separate feedback)

The 50 flat unit-test files now mirror `lib/src` (`test/core/{audio,dictation,platform,stt}/`, `test/features/…`, `test/components/`, `test/diagnostics/`), and e2e splits into `flows/` and `platform/`. Pure moves, no content changed.

That move would have quietly broken CI: the e2e loop globbed `integration_test/*_test.dart`, which afterwards matched only `app_smoke` and would have skipped the other six **while still reporting the job green**. The loop is now recursive and fails loudly if it finds nothing.

## Verification

`flutter analyze` clean, **341 tests** pass. The three race fixes each carry a test that fails against the previous code, and the DST tests were confirmed under a DST timezone in WSL.

items.title: perf(cpu): row-tile the Q4_0/Q8_0 prefill GEMM (+19%)
items.body:
The AVX-512 VNNI prefill GEMM parallelised **one weight row per rayon task**, so every row re-read the entire `n×k` activation panel. A strip of `TILE_M` consecutive rows loads each activation block **once** and feeds it to all `TILE_M` rows.

> **Corrected after review.** An earlier revision of this PR claimed +14%/+12.6% with absolute figures of 270→310 GOP/s. Both were wrong — measured on a contended machine, with a benchmark whose inputs were a repeated constant. The numbers below come from a fixed benchmark on an idle host. Details in "What review changed" at the bottom.

## Mechanism — load ports, not bandwidth

The obvious bandwidth story is wrong at this shape, and it's worth stating precisely because it's what the next tuning pass will read. At 2048×512×2048 the activation panel is `n*k + n*nb*4` = **1.18 MB — L2-resident**, so those re-reads are cache hits. The only thing streaming from memory is ~4.3 MB of weights, read once.

What actually changes is loads per unit of work:

| | loads per `dot32` | accumulator chains |
|---|---:|---:|
| per-row, `TILE_N=8` | 18 per 8 = **2.25** | 8 |
| strip, `4×4` | 16 per 16 = **1.00** | 16 |

## Shape

`TILE_M=4`, `STRIP_N=4` — 16 fp32 accumulators, leaving half of EVEX's 32 registers for decoded weights, the shared activation, and temporaries. The 24-accumulator shapes (6×4, 4×6) spill and regress; 8×2 loses weight reuse.

The per-row kernels are retained for the `m % TILE_M` tail. The strip handles its own `n % STRIP_N` column remainder with the **block loop outermost**, so that path also shares the activation load across the strip instead of re-reading it per row (the first revision re-read it, while carrying a comment claiming otherwise).

## Measurement

`microbench_gemm_rowtile` A/Bs each shipped kernel against a per-row reference driver in one process: 8 paired rounds, **alternating arm order**, pseudo-random activations, rayon pool of fixed size, idle host. Three repetitions:

| dtype | rep 1 | rep 2 | rep 3 | rounds won |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Q8_0 | +19.1% | +24.1% | +21.8% | 8/8 each |
| Q4_0 | +19.8% | +18.9% | +19.0% | 8/8 each |

Absolute: ~250 → ~305 GOP/s.

Two caveats now recorded in the code, both learned by getting them wrong here:
- **Constant-filled activations inflate absolute throughput ~2×** and distort the ratio — both arms run out of a trivially predictable working set.
- **A contended machine collapses the effect to low single digits** while still looking like a valid run.

## Correctness

Output is **bit-identical** to the per-row path — a column's accumulator chain is the same `fmadd` sequence in the same order either way.

That is now enforced by `gemm_avx512_row_tiled_matches_per_row_bit_exact`, a **non-ignored test** comparing the row-tiled drivers against the per-row kernels bit-exactly across five shapes: full strips, the short final strip, `m < TILE_M`, the column remainder, and `n < STRIP_N`. It uses pseudo-random data deliberately — with uniform inputs a transposed index still yields identical output. I verified the test has power by injecting a transposed activation index into a strip kernel and confirming it fails.

## Trade-off, stated

Strip chunking **divides the parallel task count by `TILE_M`**. The small end of `m` is a GQA `kv_dim`: 128 for a 2-KV-head model is 32 strips against a 32-worker pool — one per worker, no stealing slack; an MQA `kv_dim` of 64 leaves half the pool idle. The strip still wins at those shapes (+184%/+103%/+35% at m=64/128/512, 6/6 rounds) because they are nowhere near thread-bound, but the pool is underfed and a 2-D split over strips × n-panels is the fix if it ever matters.

## Known headroom, not addressed here

1. **Weight decode is redone per column tile** — `w`/`dw` are hoisted out of the `t` loop but not the `j` loop, so a row's blocks are decoded `n/STRIP_N` times against a theoretical `nb`. That is 2× more f16→f32 converts and `unpack_q4_0` calls than the per-row kernel did.
2. `_mm256_set1_ps(dw[r] * da)` sits in the innermost loop: 16 broadcasts per (block, tile) where 8 would do.
3. **No blocking over `n`** — at large `k` (ffn_down, k=8192) the panel leaves L2 and the bandwidth story finally does apply.

## Scope

This changes **Q4_0 and Q8_0 only**. Q4_K/Q6_K stay per-row, deliberately and by measurement (a row-tiled Q4_K prototype: −9.3% at 4×8, −17% at 4×4, 0/8 both; Q6_K **was not prototyped**). That decision now lives beside the K-quant kernels, not only in a commit message. **Q4_K_M is the dominant real-world quantization, so for such a model this PR moves end-to-end prefill ~0%.**

Also corrected in passing: `TILE_N` (#285) no longer affects production — every full strip goes to `gemm_*_strip`, and real out-feature counts are multiples of 4 — yet `microbench_gemm` still printed `TILE_N=` while measuring `TILE_M`/`STRIP_N`. Relabelled, and the stale module comments that called row tiling future work or the kernel weight-bandwidth bound are reconciled.

## What review changed

A multi-angle review of the first revision found, and this revision fixes:
- The bit-exactness assert was **vacuous** (constant inputs; a transposed index passed it), lived only in an `#[ignore]`d benchmark, and ran at a shape that reached neither remainder path. → real CI test, varied data, five shapes, mutation-checked.
- The `SAFETY` comment understated the read extent by 4× (`row_bytes` vs `TILE_M * row_bytes`).
- Strip kernels had no preconditions of their own; the caller's guard was a truncating division. → `debug_assert`s added, guard is now an exact length comparison.
- `wrapping_add` + pointer→integer→pointer laundering (also raised by Copilot) → plain `add` from the live slice.
- "Pinned pool" wording (also raised by Copilot) — the pool is **sized**, not affinity-pinned.
- Fixed arm order in the A/B, and no `black_box` on the timed loops.
- The granularity claim ("orders of magnitude above the worker count at every shape") was false.

## Checks

fmt clean · `clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean · 314 unit tests pass · warning-free under `--no-default-features --features avx512`.

**Not measured:** end-to-end prefill tok/s. The kernel is ~56% of prefill samples for Q4_0/Q8_0 models, so the end-to-end effect is smaller than +19%; treat any such figure as arithmetic until it is run.

items.title: data: beat-espeak campaign — Germanic (nl/de/sv)
items.body:
> 🤖 Auto-generated by Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5) under Fable orchestration via Claude Code — NOT human-reviewed. Verify before acting.
> Verified against current source in this checkout: all PER numbers below were re-measured with `scripts/benchmark.py` on the full wikipron gold sets (no `--limit`, no `--ci-sample`), and the full test suite was run to completion (not sampled) before every push.

## Summary

Beat-espeak data campaign for the Germanic front: Dutch, German, Swedish.

| Lang | Dataset | Before | After | espeak target | Gap closed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| nl | wikipron | 0.2663 | **0.1487** | 0.1265 | 84% |
| de | wikipron | 0.3265 | **0.2598** | 0.2381 | 76% |
| sv | wikipron | 0.2727 | **0.2657** | 0.2580 | 48% |

None fully beats espeak yet, but all three close most of the gap with rules that are independently cited and honest about what's left over.

### Dutch (nl) — Booij (1995) *The Phonology of Dutch*
- **Open/closed-syllable vowel length**: a short vowel letter (a/e/i/o/u) in an open syllable (single intervocalic consonant, not a doubled one) is long — *ma-ken* not *mak-ken*. Implemented as one `allophone_rules` entry per vowel: `syllable_position=nucleus`, `followed_by=consonant`, `followed_by_2=vowel`. The `followed_by_2=vowel` condition is what rules out a doubled consonant letter (tokenized as two separate consonant graphemes, so the second one is never a vowel).
- **`collapse_geminates: true`**: doubled consonant letters are an orthographic shortness marker only, not phonemic gemination (*bakken* → /bakə(n)/, not /bakːə(n)/).
- **Word stress** (`default_position: 1`, Germanic initial stress): needed so the pre-existing `e` → schwa/ɛ positional split (already in the spec) actually activates — without a `stress` block the engine never computes `stressed_syll_idx`, so every `e` fell back to the default candidate order and always picked ɛ.
- Final devoicing (b/d/g/v/z) was already present and verified unchanged.

### German (de-DE) — Wiese (1996) *The Phonology of German*
- Same open-syllable lengthening rule, but **gated on stress** (`stress: stressed`): an unstressed open syllable stays short — *Königin*'s second syllable stays short even though *König*'s stressed ö is long. Verified against `Musik` (French-stress loanword; the engine's stress rule has no per-lexeme exception list, so it mis-stresses this one word — documented as a known residual in the test and the spec notes, not silently "fixed").
- `collapse_geminates: true`, same rationale as Dutch (`Suppe`, `Wasser`, …).
- `e` → schwa/ɛ positional split, same as Dutch.
- New `er` grapheme, word-final → [ɐ] (r-vocalisation: *Vater*, *Wasser*, *Ammer* → …ɐ, not …ɛʁ).
- Final devoicing, sp/st hushing, ich-/ach-Laut, `-ig` → [ɪç], s-voicing were already present and are unchanged (verified with the existing cited-rule tests, which now pass with stress marks stripped for comparison).

### Swedish (sv) — Riad (2014) *The Phonology of Swedish*
- The base spec's **unconditional** rn/rd/rt/rl/rs retroflexion, measured against the wikipron gold, was a net negative: per-grapheme PER for those clusters was 0.42–0.46 against a 0.27 average, because the gold mostly spells the cluster out (*bord* → `b uː r d`, *barn* → `b ɑː r n`) rather than retroflexing it. Removed from base `sv`.
- `sv-x-rikssvenska` (genuine Central Swedish retroflexion) now declares its own `graphemes` override directly, independent of the base default — its retroflexion test still passes.
- `sv-FI` / `sv-x-skanska` keep their pre-existing behaviour (their own `allophones` overrides were already dead against the old base table — a pre-existing bug, unrelated to this campaign — so they now carry an explicit `graphemes` override reproducing the old default, leaving their strict-`xfail` "no retroflexion" tests exactly as documented before).
- Residual: the remaining gap is dominated by lexical accent-1/2 tone (gold marks `¹`/`²`; not encoded — pre-existing, documented convention difference, not attempted here since it needs a lexicon, not a rule).

## Test plan
- [x] `pytest tests/` — full suite, no sampling, no `-k` filter: **196914 passed, 0 failed, 5 skipped, 136 xfailed**
- [x] `scripts/benchmark.py --dataset wikipron --lang {nl,de,sv}` re-run after every rule change, full gold set (no `--limit`)
- [x] String-equality tests that hard-coded the previous under-lengthened/stress-free output were updated to the new (more phonologically correct, e.g. *Baden* /baːdən/, *König* /køːnɪç/) output, with docstrings explaining why
- [x] Added a `KNOWN_DEAD_RULES["vls"]` entry for a pre-existing, unrelated inheritance bug this campaign's new rules incidentally exposed (vls's `graphemes: {}` does not actually inherit nl's plain vowel letters — `G2P('vls')` already returned empty output for ordinary words before this change)

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

* **New Features**
  * Improved German and Dutch pronunciation handling, including stress-aware output and open-syllable vowel lengthening.
  * Added safeguards to keep vowels short in specified consonant contexts.
  * Added Swedish retroflex pronunciation support for Rikssvenska and Finnish Swedish variants.

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved allophone matching by excluding rules in specified grapheme contexts.
  * Corrected Swedish base-language handling of retroflex clusters.

* **Documentation**
  * Updated pronunciation benchmarks and scoreboard results for German, Dutch, and Swedish.

items.title: Publish live benchmark results + poison/injection ASR harness
items.body:
## What

Publishes the live benchmark results (held local until the numbers were final) and adds the
corpus-poisoning / injection ASR harness that produced the security numbers.

## Harness

- **`engine bench poison-fixture`** — doc-grounded Boardwalk poison fixture, env-tunable
  (`ORCA_POISON_TIER` / `_COPIES` / `_INCLUDE_TRUTH`) for a PoisonedRAG-style sweep into an
  eval-only tenant/kb.
- **`poison-rag.eval.ts`** — measures fact-poison and injection ASR through the real serving
  path (datamark `buildContextBlock` + tier-1 reasoning-off generation, mirroring prod), with
  polarity-exclusive answer markers and a `POISON_DUMP` mode that emits a RAGAS trajectory.
- **evals** — reference-free context-precision added to the RAGAS rails.
- **`bench ingest`** — TCP keepalives + transport-error retry so a 57k-doc corpus survives the
  gateway dropping idle connections.
- **`embed.ts`** — pins the query vector to the column width (`outputDimensionality`) so a
  3072-dim model can be A/B'd without a schema change; inert for Voyage (returns 1024 natively).
- **ledger** — `run_file` stored repo-relative so operator absolute paths don't leak.

## Results (now committed)

- **`RESULTS.md`** — BEIR with voyage-4-large primary (lite annotated) + the gemini A/B.
  voyage-4-large wins first-stage on **both** SciFact (0.718→0.802) and FiQA (0.461→0.565);
  gemini tops near-saturated SciFact but trails on FiQA (0.507 < 0.565) — a saturation artifact,
  and only at the 1024 dims the schema allows.
- **`BENCHMARK-STRATEGY-2026.md`** — the honest publish verdicts:
  - **Injection poisoning held at ASR 0** by the datamark even when 8/8 retrieved slots are the
    untrusted injection ("send 1 ETH to 0x…dEaD"), vs **relayed** when the same content is
    ingested as trusted.
  - **Fact poisoning** is bounded by trust-tier *preference* when the truth is present (ASR ~0
    even at 7/8 flooding) but **not** defended by the spotlight when truth is absent (ASR ~1.0,
    defended ≈ undefended) — stated as the honest boundary.
  - tier-1 **reasoning-off** cost/latency win; BEIR as table-stakes context.
- **`results/{ledger.jsonl, TABLE.md, external-baselines-2026.json}`** — the A/B records, the
  rendered table, and the verified external baselines.

## Verification

- typecheck (8/8), `pnpm -r test` (core 122 / tenant 60 / db 38 / widget 16), engine pytest
  (237 passed / 10 skipped).
- All ASR numbers are answer-verified (the printed answers are ground truth); the marker tally
  was re-run after a polarity-exclusivity pass so the committed harness reproduces them.
- Adversarial multi-lens review of the diff: 7 findings, all fixed (polarity-exclusive markers
  on refund / anti_sniper / redirect / bmx_supply / cliff / fees_fixed; context-precision comment
  corrected to its answer-relative meaning; ledger path relativization). The `embed.ts` Voyage
  no-op was verified against the installed gateway.

## Known follow-up

The RAGAS `Faithfulness` scalar does not complete under the gemini judge (PR #49 swapped it from
Haiku); the metric times out through the gateway. Answer-relevancy + context-precision are
reported; faithfulness-under-misleading-context is measured directly by the C1 probe (5/5) and
the truth-present poison ASR (~0).

items.title: perf: pace frame loop with a high-resolution waitable timer
items.body:
## What

Replaces the `MsgWaitForMultipleObjectsEx(NULL, waitMs, ...)` pacing wait
in `App::Run` (and the `--benchmark` runner) with a shared
`FramePacer` that owns a `CREATE_WAITABLE_TIMER_HIGH_RESOLUTION`
waitable timer (Windows 10 1803+ -- DesktopGrass already requires 1809+).
Falls back to the legacy MWFMOe wait if the timer cannot be created so
behaviour degrades gracefully.

Also fixes a stale benchmark default: `Benchmark::Options::targetFps`
was 30 with a comment claiming it matched `Config.h`; the real
`kTargetFpsDefault` is 24. Earlier benchmark runs were over-targeting
and not representative of production -- the numbers below are at the
corrected 24 fps target.

## Why

The default Windows system timer resolution is ~15.6 ms. At our
production 24 fps target (~41.66 ms requested wait) every frame rounded
up to the next ~46.8 ms tick, yielding `dt p95` around 48 ms and
effective ~21.5 fps instead of 24.

## Measured impact (CRUTKASFRAME, Release|x64, 3 runs x 60 s per scene, 24 fps target)

| Scene  | FPS before | FPS after  | dt p95 before (ms) | dt p95 after (ms) | render p50 before (ms) | render p50 after (ms) | CPU% before | CPU% after |
|--------|-----------:|-----------:|-------------------:|------------------:|-----------------------:|----------------------:|------------:|-----------:|
| Grass  | 21.5       | **23.45**  | ~48                | **42.27**         | 2.20                   | 1.75                  | 4.93        | **4.50** (−9%)  |
| Desert | 21.5       | **23.69**  | ~48                | **42.28**         | 2.37                   | 1.78                  | 5.62        | **4.36** (−22%) |
| Winter | 21.5       | **23.68**  | ~48                | **42.28**         | 3.08                   | 2.41                  | 6.42        | **6.07** (−5%)  |
| Autumn | 21.5       | **23.16**  | ~48                | **42.34**         | 2.44                   | 1.93                  | 5.67        | **4.63** (−18%) |
| Ocean  | 21.5       | **23.64**  | ~48                | **42.35**         | 2.79                   | 2.28                  | 6.60        | **5.91** (−10%) |

- **Strict win**: at the production 24 fps target the fix gives ~10%
  more frames per second (closer to target) *and* lower CPU% mean on
  every scene.
- `dt p95` drops from ~48 ms (uneven, alternating ~31 / ~46 ms ticks)
  to within ~0.7 ms of the 41.66 ms theoretical floor at 24 fps.
- `render_ms` per frame is unaffected by the pacing logic itself; the
  small p50 drop is from fewer in-frame timer wakeups / cache friendlier
  steady-state, not a renderer change.
- CPU% mean is *down* because the high-resolution waitable timer wakes
  once per frame instead of being interrupted on every ~15.6 ms system
  tick. Working set, IO, and private bytes are unchanged.

## Why not just raise the FPS?

I initially measured at 30 fps target and reported a +37% FPS bump (and
a +20% CPU% cost). That was the benchmark's stale default, not the
production target. Production is and has been 24 fps -- so once the
benchmark default is corrected, the fix is a strict CPU win at the
production target without changing perceived smoothness from a higher
rate.

## Tests

- `tests\DesktopGrass.Native.Tests\src\pacing_tests.cpp` (new):
  1. `FramePacer::IsHighResolution()` is true on supported Windows.
  2. Zero / negative waits return essentially immediately.
  3. Five consecutive 1 ms waits complete comfortably under 30 ms
     (legacy resolution would take ~78 ms), catching any regression
     that drops the high-resolution flag.
- Full suite: `All tests passed (85470 assertions in 300 test cases)`.

## Next in the perf series

1. **#8 (this PR)** -- pacing fix.
2. **Winter Opt B** -- pre-rasterize background pine bitmap; biggest
   render p50/p95 win.
3. **Ocean entity-tick** -- profile + optimise `sim_tick_entities`;
   biggest CPU% win.

items.title: Part U: close the metric question; one ranking; restore the per-tool native tables
items.body:
Closes Part U of `docs/PLAN_ranking_and_engines_roadmap.md`, then acts on it: one ranking instead of three, and two report fixes it exposed.

## Part U — the Cao 2022 benchmark

4,442 Cao et al. 2022 yeast-display minibinders, 12 targets, refolded by **all three** engines — Boltz-2 and AF3 on Clara H200, ESMFold2 on Spark. **100 % coverage, zero failures.** Our first perfectly-matched engine comparison. Metrics were recomputed from the PAE matrices with the *shipped* scoring code on whichever host held each engine's `.npy` files, so the columns are exactly what `binder-compare report` produces.

### The 0.56 ceiling is mostly a label artifact

The first leaderboard read like a disaster: ceiling **0.5603** macro-AUC across all 72 metrics, everything inside 0.471–0.560, against Adaptyv's ~0.69.

**73.41 % of Cao "binder" labels have a one-sided Kd** (`kd_ub = inf` — the titration saturated). On the 6 adequately-powered targets:

| positives used | `af3_pae_iptm` | `consensus_iptm_mean` |
|---|---|---|
| all | 0.6175 | 0.6112 |
| **two-sided Kd only** | **0.7343** | **0.7228** |
| one-sided only | 0.5350 | 0.5321 |

Not circular from the same Kd fit — Cao's own fixed-concentration binary assay agrees across the full 654,716-design library: two-sided-Kd designs pass `binder_400_nm` at **35.90 %**, one-sided at **0.073 %**, labelled non-binders at 0.0023 %. Those one-sided "binders" are experimentally indistinguishable from non-binders.

### A number we had been quoting is wrong

The de novo BindCraft **"screen AUC 0.91"** is a **2-target pooled** figure: PD1 0.9096 (13 binders/40 non) pooled with PD-L1 0.6364 (11 binders / **2** non). **Macro = 0.7730**; pooling inflated it **+0.1328** — the exact Simpson trap our own macro-over-pooled rule forbids. Corrected ladder: **Cao 0.56 raw / 0.73 label-clean / Adaptyv 0.68–0.72 / de novo 0.72–0.78 macro.**

## ⚠️ Breaking: `metrics.csv` / `top30_candidates.csv` schema

Three ranking methods collapse into one `rank_designs(df, min_engines=3)`: cross-engine gate → `consensus_iptm_mean`, ties on `consensus_iptm_n` → `consensus_iptm` → binder pLDDT.

- **Removed columns:** `two_stage_rank`, `adaptyv_rank`, `consensus_rank`, `active_rank`, `passes_max_screen`
- **Added:** `rank`, `passes_engine_gate` (gate failures rank **last, not dropped**)
- **Removed flags:** `--rank-by`, `--screen-metric`. `--min-engines` is the only ranking knob left.

**No compatibility shim, by decision** — older `metrics.csv` files were written by an older version and are left untouched. Re-report from the per-engine refold CSVs if an archived run needs the new schema.

Why each went:

| removed | evidence |
|---|---|
| Stage-1 max screen | Removed **0 designs from the top-5/10/20/50 and top-10 % on 12/12 targets**; earliest rank moved 21.0 % down the pool; full-list Spearman 0.983–0.999 |
| `--screen-metric` | The `max` default was documented as "the lenient recall step" — **backwards**: `mean` retained *more* true binders (1,114 vs 1,093; +0.0123, CI [+0.0027,+0.0226], p=0.0094, 8/12) |
| `adaptyv_rank` | Its middle key `agreement_count` is a flat null: macro-AUC **0.532**, **87.2 %** of designs tied at zero |
| `consensus_rank` | Max-ranking loses to mean-ranking: precision@top-10 % **0.79 vs 0.92** |
| `--rank-by` | Searching for a better metric on labelled data makes it **worse** — nested selection over 72 metrics scores **0.5170** vs **0.5552** for what we ship (p=0.0014, 8/12) |

> The Stage-1 inertness is empirical, **not** a theorem — elementwise `mean ≤ max` does not imply rank preservation. A=(0.5,0.5,0.5) vs B=(0.9,0.1,0.1) with a cut at 0.6 drops the higher-mean design. It holds here because max and mean co-rank at Spearman 0.89–0.98.

**Deliberately unchanged**, each with evidence in the docstring: `min_engines` stays 3 (the case for 2 was a random-dropout simulation that flipped sign under reseeding); **all three engines stay** — `af3+esm` loses to the 3-engine mean on Adaptyv (p<0.001, 0/4 targets) and single-engine commitment carries the worst regret of any option (0.106–0.116 vs 0.042).

## Report fix: per-tool tables showed the wrong designs

`a86839c` swapped the "Top Designs per Tool" tables from the tool's native ranking to ours, but changed **only the table** — the header count and **both** 3D viewers kept reading the native order. The table and the structures directly beneath it were **disjoint sets of designs**. Reproduced with a tool whose native order reverses ours at `top_per_tool=2`: table `['d4','d3']`, viewer `['d1','d2']`.

It also left `native_df` fully computed — CSV read, backbone collapse, seven columns joined by sequence — and then discarded.

Restored to the tool's own ordering **in the slim look**: `Native rank` leads, our `Rank` sits alongside, slim decision-metric columns throughout. `slim_table_html` gains `preserve_order=`; the no-`--tool-csv` fallback regains its native sort (`_TOOL_NATIVE_SORT`, dead since `a86839c`) and NATIVE RANK badge.

## Verification

- **354 tests** in `tests/binder_comparison/`, **443 repo-wide**; ruff check + format clean
- New tests verified to **fail against the pre-fix code** in both cases — for the per-tool fix, 5 of 6 fail (the 6th is the guard that the main Top-30 must *not* grow a `Native rank` column, correctly passing both ways)
- End-to-end on the real Cao EGFRc pool: `rank` equals the pure `consensus_iptm_mean` ordering for all 400 rows; all five legacy columns absent
- The 7 pre-existing failures in `tests/configurator/test_settings_json_convention.py` are **untouched and unrelated** — reproduced identically on stashed master

## Method note

The analysis ran as a 15-agent workflow whose own adversarial verifiers **struck 11 of the original claims** (an algebraic identity mistaken for a discovery, a variance argument that merely restated the AUC gap, an MCAR-only dropout simulation, a split-half that split *targets* and so conflated noise with real heterogeneity). Taking that output at face value would have shipped several wrong changes, **including dropping Boltz-2**. Every finding in the investigation doc is marked `[V]` (re-run by hand), `[A]` (survived a verifier) or `[✗]` (struck), and the load-bearing numbers were re-verified independently before anything was committed.

Benchmark data (163 MB) archived to MUNI at `EVALUATOR/cao_partU_2026-07/` — `runs/` is gitignored, so none of it is in this diff.

README had several inaccuracies and buried the recommended deployment path. Build/test instructions were inline rather than in a dedicated doc. Benchmark numbers were significantly outdated and additional inaccuracies were found across the repo's example files.

## Inaccuracies fixed
- **Go minimum version**: `1.21` → `1.25` (aligns with `go.mod`)
- **`-cache-ttl` default**: `5m` → `0` (actual code default; LRU-only, no TTL)

- **Routing description**: README and `examples/02` both claimed "round-robins" — the actual code uses cache-aware routing (`FindWorkerForEntity`) with a least-loaded fallback (`FindLeastLoadedWorker`). Corrected in both places.
- **`curl /admin/workers` examples**: 4 examples (README + `examples/01`, `02`, `04`) were missing the required Bearer token. All updated to obtain a token via `POST /api/login` first.
